follow.a: The message you would send anyway. Here, any sign beat no sign, which a test against silence would have mistaken for a norm effect.

A smiley face kept efficient homes steady
challenges.answerTitle: A norm message can backfire
challenges.explain: Schultz and colleagues gave usage feedback to 290 San Marcos households. Below-average homes shown only the neighborhood average raised daily use from 10.15 to 11.13 kWh over the longer term; adding a smiley-face approval cue held them at baseline.
challenges.implication: When sending peer comparisons, add explicit approval for customers already doing better than average, and check in a pilot whether low users drift up.
challenges.boundary: Two doorhanger messages to 290 California households, with electricity read from meters over about four weeks.

follow.a: 290 households in San Marcos, California, with visible electricity meters; 287 stayed in the analysis.
Below-average households that saw only the neighborhood average rose from 10.38 to 11.27 kWh per day in the first week, and stayed higher three weeks later.

Above-average households given only the average cut 1.22 kWh per day in the first week. Over the longer term their use was 21.29 kWh per day against a 22.32 baseline, a drop that was not statistically significant.

chart.note: Daily electricity use of below-average homes, kWh per day.

challenges.title: Fixing a slow process
challenges.scene: In experiments, people were asked to improve things such as a Lego structure, a mini-golf hole or a written essay, and could change them by adding or by removing elements.
challenges.question: Which kind of fix do people tend to miss?
options: Adding a review step
Removing an existing step
Automating an existing step
challenges.answerTitle: Subtraction is often missed
challenges.explain: In Adams, Converse, Hales and Klotz's experiment 4, only 21% of uncued participants listed any subtractive idea for improving a mini-golf hole. Reminded that they could add or subtract, 48% did.
challenges.implication: Make “What can we remove?” mandatory in process reviews.
challenges.boundary: Eight experiments with puzzles and design tasks in which removing an element was an advantageous change.

follow.a: Problems such as stabilizing a Lego structure, improving a miniature golf course, and transforming a grid pattern. Most people added a block to the Lego structure rather than removing one.
Hundreds of participants across eight experiments, each solving a different improvement problem.
Being cued to consider subtraction, and having several chances rather than one to see that adding was not working.

chart.note: Share listing at least one idea that removes something, experiment 4.

challenges.title: Under pressure
challenges.scene: In one experiment, people improved a pattern on a grid; some did it while keeping track of a second task at the same time.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Pressure favors additions
challenges.explain: Across eight experiments, Adams, Converse, Hales and Klotz found people were less likely to spot helpful subtractive changes under higher cognitive load, and also when nothing cued subtraction or when they had only one chance to notice it.
challenges.implication: Schedule deliberate simplification sessions with fewer distractions.
challenges.boundary: Cognitive load was manipulated in controlled experiments on puzzle and design tasks.

follow.a: Yes. People found subtractive improvements more often when they had several opportunities, rather than one, to notice that adding was not working.

follow.q: Which real problems do the authors link this to?
follow.a: Overloaded schedules, institutional red tape, and damage to the environment.
No. It was one of eight experiments that all pointed to a default toward adding.

forecast.claim: People juggling other tasks were more likely to overlook improvements that remove something.

challenges.title: The wheel of fortune
challenges.scene: People spun a wheel that landed on 10 or 65, then estimated the share of UN member countries that are African. The group that saw 65 gave a median of 45%.
challenges.question: What median estimate did the group that saw 10 give?
challenges.answerTitle: 25%, pulled down by a random number
challenges.explain: Median estimates were 25% after the wheel showed 10 and 45% after it showed 65, though everyone could see the number was random.
challenges.implication: In negotiations and forecasts, write down your own estimate before you see anyone else’s number.
challenges.boundary: People estimating percentages after watching a wheel produce a visibly random number; paying for accuracy did not reduce the effect.

follow.a: The wheel was spun in front of them. They first said whether the true value was higher or lower than the number, then gave their own estimate.

follow.q: Does anchoring show up in calculations too?
follow.a: Yes. High school students given 5 seconds estimated 1x2x...x8 at a median of 512 and 8x7x...x1 at 2,250. The correct answer is 40,320.
No. The authors note that experienced researchers are prone to the same biases when they think intuitively.

estimate.label: Median estimate after seeing 10

chart.note: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), p. 1128.

challenges.title: Tight, loose or split
challenges.scene: Two teams have the same average cooperation. In one, behavior is tightly clustered around the average; in the other, it is widely spread out.
challenges.question: Which two results did the experiments find?
options: Loose norms generated more behavioral variation
The spread of behavior shaped choices
The average of what others did explained choices
Tight norms produced the most extreme choices
challenges.answerTitle: The spread of others’ behavior changed choices
challenges.explain: Dimant, Gelfand, Hochleitner and Sonderegger showed about 1,200 Americans co-player behavior with the same mean but different spreads. Choices tracked the spread: contribution variance was 1.26 after a tight norm and 1.65 after a loose one.
challenges.implication: Report the spread and clustering of team behavior alongside averages in culture and engagement dashboards.
challenges.boundary: Two-player contribution game with 1,203 US adults, varying the shape of the norm while holding its average fixed.

follow.a: They played a two-player public goods game. Each could contribute up to four tokens; contributions were multiplied by 1.4 and shared.
About 1,200 US participants recruited on Prolific, representative by age, gender, and ethnicity.

follow.q: Why does this matter for a manager?
follow.a: Two teams with the same average norm can behave very differently once the spread of views differs, so report the spread as well as the mean.

study.design: Online experiment, two-player contribution game (6 treatments)

chart.note: Variance of contributions after seeing others' choices.

challenges.title: Comfort with campus drinking
challenges.scene: Students rated their own comfort with campus drinking and the comfort of the average student at their university.
challenges.question: What did students report?
options: Peers were as comfortable as they were
Peers were more comfortable than they were
Peers were less comfortable with drinking than they were
challenges.answerTitle: Private views and public beliefs diverge
challenges.explain: In all four of Prentice and Miller's studies, students rated their peers as more comfortable with campus drinking than they were themselves. Over a semester, men shifted their own attitudes toward that mistaken norm; women did not.
challenges.implication: Elicit private views before public discussion.
challenges.boundary: Four studies of college students' own attitudes toward campus alcohol use and their estimates of peers' attitudes.

follow.a: College students, across four studies, who rated their own comfort with campus drinking and estimated the average student's comfort.
In a study that followed students over a semester, men shifted their attitudes toward the norm they mistakenly perceived. Women did not.

follow.q: What did feeling out of step cost?
follow.a: Students who saw themselves as deviant felt more alienated from campus, even though that deviance was illusory.

study.design: Four studies, one following students over a semester

challenges.title: Drawing a party’s norm
challenges.scene: Members of a political party agree on its headline position. Researchers asked members to draw how views are spread within their party.
challenges.question: What did drawing each party’s norm reveal?
options: Near-uniform views held by members of each party
Two opposed camps within each party
Several coexisting views within each party
challenges.answerTitle: Each party holds several distinct views
challenges.explain: Among 996 US respondents, Panizza, Dimant, Kimbrough and Vostroknutov recovered several views within each party. Agreement ranged from 95% of Democrats including the same view on same-sex rights in their drawings to only 50% of Republicans on gun policy.
challenges.implication: Before engaging a stakeholder group, map the distinct views inside it and estimate each view's share.
challenges.boundary: One incentivized online survey of 996 US respondents on seven political issues, compared with a standard single-norm measure.

follow.a: 996 US respondents on Prolific, stratified by age, gender, and political orientation.
Abortion, same-sex rights, marijuana legalization, federal spending, gun violence, immigration, and energy investments.
Respondents sketch the views different subgroups might hold and estimate the share holding each. Pay depends on how close their guesses come.

chart.note: Share of a party including the same view in their drawing, the highest and the lowest issue.

challenges.title: Which network spreads change?
challenges.scene: In an online health community, researchers built networks that were either clustered (neighbors share neighbors) or random (more long-range ties), then seeded a health behavior.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Reinforcement can beat reach
challenges.explain: In Centola's online experiment with 1,528 participants, a health behavior reached 53.77% of people in clustered networks but only 38.26% in random networks, and it spread more than four times faster through the clustered ones.
challenges.implication: Launch hard-to-adopt practices inside tightly connected teams, so each person hears about them from several colleagues.
challenges.boundary: 1,528 anonymous online participants in constructed networks deciding whether to register for a health forum.

follow.q: How much farther did it spread?
follow.a: The behavior reached 53.77% of people in clustered networks, against 38.26% in random networks.
Diffusion in clustered networks was more than four times faster than in random ones.
Yes. Fewer than 15% of adopters who got one signal returned to the forum, against over 30% of those who got two.

forecast.claim: Behavior spread farther through random long ties than through clustered ties.

chart.note: Share of people who adopted the health behavior.

challenges.title: Does turn-taking make groups smart?
challenges.scene: A 2010 Science paper reported a general “collective intelligence” factor in groups, linked to members’ social sensitivity and to equal turn-taking in conversation. Independent researchers ran their own groups.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Turn-taking did not predict it; members’ IQ did
challenges.explain: In the independent replication, members’ individual IQ largely accounted for differences in group performance, and the turn-taking and share-of-women effects were not supported.
challenges.implication: Treat team-composition recipes from single studies as hypotheses. Track your own teams’ results before redesigning how meetings run.
challenges.boundary: Lab groups on standardized tasks. The original team’s later meta-analysis of 22 studies supports a collective intelligence factor, so the debate continues.

follow.q: What did the original paper claim?
follow.a: Woolley et al. (2010) reported a general factor across group tasks, correlated with average social sensitivity, equal turn-taking and the share of women.
No. The original team’s 2021 meta-analysis supports the factor and points to social perceptiveness, while independent analyses find it weaker or explained by members’ IQ.
Team-design advice spread widely from the original paper. When an independent test fails on the key predictors, the advice should wait for more evidence.

forecast.claim: Groups with more equal conversational turn-taking scored higher on collective intelligence.

challenges.title: Identical résumé, different name
challenges.scene: In a field experiment, comparable résumés were assigned names signaling different racial identities.
challenges.question: Approximately how much higher was the callback rate for White-sounding names?
challenges.answerTitle: 50% more callbacks
challenges.explain: Bertrand and Mullainathan answered Boston and Chicago help-wanted ads with fictitious résumés randomly given African-American- or White-sounding names. White names received 50 percent more callbacks, and callbacks responded more to résumé quality for White names.
challenges.implication: Run periodic paired-résumé audits of your own screening, comparing callbacks for identical profiles with different names.
challenges.boundary: Fictitious résumés sent to sales, administrative, clerical, and customer-service ads in Boston and Chicago, 2001 to 2002.

follow.q: Was the gap the same across jobs?
follow.a: Yes. The racial gap was uniform across occupation, industry and employer size.

follow.q: Did a stronger résumé close the gap?
follow.a: No. Better credentials raised callbacks much less for African-American names than for White names.
No. Employers who listed that label in their ads discriminated as much as other employers.

estimate.label: Callback advantage (%)

study.n: Fictitious résumés sent to help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago

challenges.title: Screens at auditions
challenges.scene: Orchestra auditions begin concealing candidates’ identity behind screens.
challenges.question: How did the authors characterize their evidence?
challenges.answerTitle: Favorable to women, with some imprecise estimates
challenges.explain: Goldin and Rouse estimate that the screen raised by 50 percent the chance a woman advanced from certain preliminary rounds, and that blind auditions explain about 30 percent of the rise in women among new hires. Some estimates have large standard errors.
challenges.implication: Hide names and other identity cues in early screening rounds, then compare pass rates by group before and after.
challenges.boundary: Orchestra audition records; the authors report large standard errors for several estimates, and one effect ran in the opposite direction.

follow.a: Mixed. The authors note that some estimates have large standard errors and one effect persistently runs against women; they judge that the weight of the evidence favors women.
That blind auditions fostered impartiality in hiring and contributed to the rising share of women in orchestras.
With actual audition records, comparing the same musicians across auditions with and without a screen.

study.design: Panel of audition records (individual fixed effects)
study.n: Musicians auditioning at major US orchestras

options: Favorable to women, precisely estimated
Mixed by round, precisely estimated
Favorable to women, with imprecise estimates
Unfavorable to women, mostly in early rounds

challenges.title: Why did they stay away?
challenges.scene: White and Black participants were asked how interested they were in contact with the other group, and why each side might hold back.
challenges.question: How did each group explain the hesitation?
options: Own side fears rejection; other lacks interest
Each side said it feared open conflict
Both sides feared rejection; neither lacked interest
challenges.answerTitle: The misreading can be mutual
challenges.explain: Across seven studies, Shelton and Richeson found that White and Black participants wanted more contact with the other group but believed it did not. Each explained its own hesitation by fear of racial rejection and the other side's by lack of interest.
challenges.implication: Have managers make the first cross-group introduction, so neither side has to risk reaching out first.
challenges.boundary: Seven studies of White and Black participants' interest in interracial contact and how they explained avoidance.

follow.a: White and Black participants, across seven studies.
Both groups privately wanted more contact, yet each wrongly believed the other group did not.

follow.q: Did the researchers go beyond attitudes?
follow.a: Yes. One study examined the behavioral consequences of the bias, and a final study tested a way to reduce it based on the extended contact hypothesis.

challenges.title: Is loss aversion a law?
challenges.scene: A workshop leader says: “Losses always hurt more than equal gains feel good.”
challenges.question: Which two statements fit the loss-aversion evidence?
options: Loss aversion held steady when gamble ranges changed
Loss aversion can reverse in experiments
The distributions of outcomes can matter
challenges.answerTitle: It is not a universal law
challenges.explain: Experiments have found that apparent loss aversion can disappear or reverse when distributions change.
challenges.implication: Before applying a 2:1 loss-aversion rule to pricing, test how customers respond to the gains and losses they actually face.
challenges.boundary: Accept-or-reject choices on 50/50 money gambles, mostly hypothetical, with Mechanical Turk workers and Warwick students.

follow.a: People accepted or rejected 50/50 gambles offering a gain and a loss. The researchers varied the ranges from which gains and losses were drawn.
Three online experiments with Mechanical Turk workers (323 to 401 analyzed) using hypothetical gambles, and one lab study with 82 Warwick participants playing for real money.
It is contested. Andre and de Langhe (2021) showed the conditions used different gambles; comparing only shared gambles removes the pattern.

study.n: 1,106 MTurk workers and 82 lab participants analyzed

challenges.title: Hate or love?
challenges.scene: Across 15 experiments, Trump supporters and opponents rated how close they felt to each side, then chose whether to give money to, or take money from, members of each side.
challenges.question: Where did in-group love and out-group hate show up?
options: Hate showed in feelings, love in behavior
Love showed in feelings, hate in behavior
Love and hate showed mainly in feelings
challenges.answerTitle: Closer to allies, but no more generous to them
challenges.explain: In Dimant’s experiments, Trump supporters and opponents felt far closer to their own side (78.1%) than to a group-mate who shared only a painting preference (about 39%), yet gave allies no more money (14.97% versus 13.54%). From opponents, they took 22.9%.
challenges.implication: When teams distrust each other, measure how they actually treat each other, not only how they feel about each other.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized behavioral experiments with US Trump supporters and opponents, plus a sports-identity comparison.

follow.q: How large was the evidence base?
follow.a: Five preregistered studies with 15 behavioral experiments and over 8,600 participants.
The studies compared political identity with other political and nonpolitical identities.
How people helped, harmed and cooperated with members of each group in incentivized games.
Giving and taking games, in which one person moved money to or from another; a public goods game in the same project measured cooperation separately.

chart.note: Share of the endowment given or taken.

challenges.title: Nudges across the divide
challenges.scene: A leader offers prosocial defaults and normative messages to participants divided by political identity.
challenges.question: Which two results did the nudges produce?
options: The interventions improved prosociality
The nudges closed the partisan gap on most measures
Measured polarization gaps persisted
The norm nudge worked; the default did not
challenges.answerTitle: General improvement, persistent gap
challenges.explain: With a default nudge, Dimant shows that taking from political opponents fell from about 20% of the endowment to essentially 0%, and giving to allies rose from about 10–15% to 25–35%. The ally-opponent difference stayed highly significant (p < 0.001).
challenges.implication: Track between-group gaps as a separate metric when testing interventions, since average cooperation can rise while the gap stays.
challenges.boundary: Default and norm nudges tested in incentivized giving and cooperation games with US Trump supporters and opponents.

follow.a: A default nudge and a norm nudge that gave descriptive information about others' behavior.

follow.q: How large was the evidence base?
follow.a: Five preregistered studies with 15 experiments and over 8,600 participants.

follow.q: What does this mean for a manager?
follow.a: Raising overall goodwill can leave the gap between groups in place, so track the gap itself, not only the average.

challenges.title: Same average, two teams
challenges.scene: Two departments report the same average rating of how acceptable a practice is. You suspect their norms still differ.
challenges.question: How do you check whether their norms differ?
options: Ask each team’s manager to describe the norm
Compare how often each team breaks the rule
Survey a larger sample and compare averages
Ask each person how views are spread across colleagues
challenges.answerTitle: Keep the whole distribution
challenges.explain: Dimant's method elicits, with incentives, each person's belief about the full distribution of views instead of the mean or most common view, so a unified team and one split into opposing camps can be told apart.
challenges.implication: In culture surveys, ask each person how views are spread across colleagues, not only what the typical view is.
challenges.boundary: A short methods paper presenting an incentive-compatible survey tool that measures each person's perceived norm distribution.

follow.q: What do standard norm measures capture?
follow.a: The average or most frequent behavior or opinion in a given context.
The method is incentive-compatible, so respondents are rewarded for reporting their real beliefs about how views are spread.
Yes. The paper comes with ready-made Qualtrics software.

challenges.title: Same numbers, other frame
challenges.scene: A disease will kill 600 people. Framed as lives saved, 72% chose a sure plan (200 saved) over a gamble. Others saw the same plans framed as deaths: 400 die for sure, or a one-third chance nobody dies.
challenges.question: In the deaths frame, what share chose the gamble?
challenges.answerTitle: 78% gambled once the frame was losses
challenges.explain: With identical outcomes, 72% chose the sure option when it was framed as lives saved; 78% chose the gamble when the same options were framed as deaths.
challenges.implication: In investment memos, state each option's outcomes as both gains and losses before the team decides.
challenges.boundary: Stanford and UBC students choosing between hypothetical public-health programs in a classroom questionnaire.

follow.a: Students at Stanford and the University of British Columbia, in brief classroom questionnaires: 152 saw the lives-saved version and 155 the deaths version.

follow.q: Do experts fall for it too?
follow.a: Yes. The authors report the same reversal in other groups, including university faculty and physicians.

follow.q: Why does the frame flip choices?
follow.a: People tend to avoid risk when outcomes are described as gains and to take risk when they are described as losses.

estimate.label: Share choosing the gamble in the deaths frame

chart.note: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), p. 453; N = 152 and 155.

challenges.title: Who should have the final say?
challenges.scene: You are designing workflows for two AI-supported tasks. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments shows when humans plus AI beat either one working alone.
challenges.question: For each task, who should do the work?

tasks.text: Flag fake hotel reviews: AI is 73% accurate, staff 55%
tasks.why: In this example the human-AI team scored 69%, below the AI alone at 73%.

tasks.text: Classify bird photos: staff are 81% accurate, AI 73%
tasks.why: Here the human-AI team reached 90%, beating both humans and AI alone.

challenges.answerTitle: Combine only where humans beat the AI
challenges.explain: Across 370 effect sizes, human-AI teams did worse than the best performer alone (g = −0.23). They gained when humans beat the AI (g = 0.46) and lost when the AI was better (g = −0.54).
challenges.implication: Benchmark humans and AI separately before adding a human review layer; skip that layer where the AI alone is clearly stronger.
challenges.boundary: Covers experiments published January 2020 to June 2023 across very different tasks; the averages describe that range of tasks.

follow.q: Do humans with AI beat humans alone?
follow.a: Yes. Against humans alone, human-AI systems performed better (g = 0.64). The losses appear only against the better of the two.
Decision tasks, where people choose from a fixed set of options, showed losses (g = −0.27). Creation tasks trended positive (g = 0.19, not significant).

follow.q: Where do the review and bird numbers come from?
follow.a: Both come from Cabrera, Perer and Hong (2023), which the authors discuss to show how relative skill drives synergy.

challenges.title: Control over the model
challenges.scene: In an incentivized task, people forecast students' math percentiles. They may use an imperfect model that outperforms human forecasts, but each group gets different rules for adjusting it.
challenges.question: Which group chose to use the model least often?
options: Could adjust each forecast, though by up to 2
Could not change the model at all
Could adjust each forecast by up to 10
challenges.answerTitle: Any control beats none; size barely matters
challenges.explain: In Study 2, 47% used the unchangeable model versus 68% to 71% when they could adjust it by 2, 5 or 10 percentiles. The two adjustable groups did not differ meaningfully, so their order is not scored.
challenges.implication: Let staff make small, bounded adjustments to model outputs instead of mandating the outputs unchanged.
challenges.boundary: Online and lab forecasting of student test percentiles with small bonuses.

follow.a: No. Because more people used the model, participants who could modify it forecast more accurately as a result, the authors report.
Also 71%, the same as the 10-percentile limit. More freedom did not raise uptake.
Yes. Being able to modify the model raised satisfaction, belief that the model was superior, and willingness to use algorithms for later forecasts.

chart.note: Share who chose to use the model, Study 2.

challenges.title: Same jail rate, less crime
challenges.scene: Judges decide whether defendants await trial at home or in jail, partly by predicting crime risk. Researchers train a machine-learning model on past cases and simulate letting it rank defendants.
challenges.question: Holding the jailing rate fixed, how much could crime fall?

estimate.label: Maximum crime reduction at the same jailing rate

challenges.answerTitle: Up to 24.7% less crime
challenges.explain: Simulations showed crime reductions up to 24.7% with no change in jailing rates, or jailing cuts up to 41.9% with no rise in crime.
challenges.implication: Audit high-volume screening decisions with a prediction model and estimate how many errors you could cut at today's approval rate.
challenges.boundary: Policy simulations on past bail cases; crime outcomes exist only for released defendants.

study.design: Machine-learning policy simulation on court records

follow.q: Couldn't the model just copy judges' choices?
follow.a: Crime is observed only for defendants judges released. The authors use methods such as quasi-random assignment of cases to judges to compare fairly.
The authors report these gains can be achieved while also reducing racial disparities.

follow.q: Is there another way to use the gain?
follow.a: Yes. Hold crime constant and jail fewer people: jailing could fall up to 41.9% with no increase in crime.

challenges.title: The formula versus the expert
challenges.scene: A meta-analysis compares expert clinicians' predictions about human health and behavior with predictions from statistical formulas.
challenges.question: On average, how much more accurate were the formulas?

estimate.label: Average accuracy advantage of formulas over experts

challenges.answerTitle: About 10% more accurate
challenges.explain: Across 136 studies, formulas were about 10% more accurate on average. Experts were substantially more accurate in only 6% to 16% of studies.
challenges.implication: For repeated predictions from structured data, make a validated scoring rule the default and log every expert override.
challenges.boundary: Studies of clinical and behavioral prediction up to 2000 using statistical formulas; many studies showed ties.

follow.a: No. The formula advantage held across judgment tasks, types of judges, judges' experience and types of data.

follow.q: Do interviews give experts an edge?
follow.a: The reverse. Clinical predictions did relatively worse when predictors included clinical interview data.

follow.q: How often did formulas win clearly?
follow.a: Formulas substantially outperformed experts in 33% to 47% of studies. In many others the two were about equally accurate.

challenges.title: Who gets extra care?
challenges.scene: A health system uses a widely sold algorithm to choose patients for an extra-care program.
challenges.question: Why were Black patients flagged less than equally sick White patients?
options: Less is spent on Black patients at equal need
The model used zip code as a proxy for race
The model had too little training data
Race was an input to the model

dag.alt: Health need and race both affect spending. The risk score is trained to predict spending, so lower spending on Black patients lowers their scores at the same need.

labels: If the spending gap were removed (simulated)
chart.note: Share of Black patients flagged for extra help.

challenges.answerTitle: Cost was a biased proxy for need
challenges.explain: Less money is spent caring for Black patients, so predicted cost understated their need. Removing the disparity would raise their share of extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%.
challenges.implication: Before deploying a model, confirm its target measures what you care about, and audit outcomes by group at equal scores.
challenges.boundary: One widely used commercial algorithm in US health care; the size of the bias depends on spending gaps in each system.

study.design: Audit of a widely used health-care risk algorithm
study.n: Patients at one large academic hospital

follow.a: Reformulating the algorithm so it no longer used costs as a proxy for needs eliminated the racial bias in predicting who needs extra care.
At a given risk score, Black patients were sicker than White patients, and the bias cut the number of Black patients identified for extra care by more than half.

follow.q: Why did cost seem a sensible target?
follow.a: The authors note that health-care cost appears to be an effective proxy for health on many measures, which made the problem easy to miss.

challenges.title: When managers overrule the test
challenges.scene: Fifteen firms hiring low-skilled service workers introduce a job test that scores applicants. Managers can still hire against its recommendations.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Hires made against the test’s recommendation more often turned out worse.

challenges.answerTitle: Overruling the test went with worse hires
challenges.explain: Across 15 firms that introduced job testing for low-skilled service workers, Hoffman, Kahn and Li found that managers facing similar applicant pools who hired against test recommendations ended up with worse average hires.
challenges.implication: Track override rates by manager, compare outcomes of overridden hires, and require a written reason for each override.
challenges.boundary: Low-skilled service jobs at 15 firms adopting job testing.

follow.a: The authors conclude managers often overrule test recommendations because they are biased or mistaken, not mainly because they hold better information.

follow.q: What tradeoff does the firm face?
follow.a: More weight on test scores can cut bias and error but may discard useful private information held by managers. Here the first effect dominated.
The authors compared managers facing similar applicant pools, so differences in overrides did not come from differences in who applied.

challenges.title: Spot the AI profile
challenges.scene: Readers see self-descriptions written for job, hospitality and dating profiles. Some were written by people, others by an AI language model.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: People told AI-written from human-written self-descriptions apart well above chance.

challenges.answerTitle: Detection was at chance: 50 to 52%
challenges.explain: Across experiments with 4,600 participants, people identified the source with only 50 to 52% accuracy, relying on cues like first-person pronouns and family topics.
challenges.implication: Do not count on reviewers to spot AI-written applications or reviews; set disclosure rules and verify claims directly.
challenges.boundary: Short self-presentations in professional, hospitality and dating contexts, judged by online participants.

follow.a: No. In the dating context half the participants were offered a $3 accuracy bonus, with no difference in performance.

follow.q: Can AI text seem more human than human?
follow.a: Yes. Text optimized against people's cues was judged human 65.7% of the time, versus 51.7% for real human text.
First-person pronouns, contractions and family topics were read as signs of a human writer, but they did not reliably indicate one.

challenges.title: Who argues your case?
challenges.scene: In 10-minute online debates on assigned topics, people faced either a human or GPT-4. Some opponents also received basic demographic details about the person they debated. The options below are compared with debates between two people.
challenges.question: Which opponent shifted agreement most? Spread 100 points by how likely each is.
options: GPT-4
GPT-4 with demographic profile
Human with demographic profile
challenges.answerTitle: Personalized GPT-4 was most persuasive
challenges.explain: Versus human-human debates, personalized GPT-4 raised the odds of higher post-debate agreement by 81.2%. GPT-4 without profiles and personalized humans showed no significant effect.
challenges.implication: Treat customer data fed to persuasive AI as a governed input; review consent and disclosure before using it in sales.
challenges.boundary: Short structured online debates with assigned positions and basic demographics.

follow.q: How often did personalized GPT-4 win?

follow.q: Could people tell they faced an AI?

follow.q: Did humans use the profile well?

challenges.title: The cost of an AI label

challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Less believed and less shared
challenges.explain: Across 4,976 participants, the label cut perceived accuracy and sharing whether headlines were true or false, human- or AI-made. The effect was three times smaller than a 'false' label.
challenges.implication: If you label AI use, state what the AI did; vague labels read as full automation and penalize accurate content.
challenges.boundary: Headlines shown to US and UK online participants; the penalty disappeared when labels came with weak or medium definitions of AI involvement.

follow.a: Readers expected AI-labeled headlines to be written entirely by AI. Without a definition, they leaned toward assuming full automation.
In Study 2 the labels had no significant effect when readers got weak or medium definitions. The penalty remained with no definition or a strong one.
Yes. Human-made headlines wrongly labeled as AI-generated were also rated lower.

forecast.claim: Labeling headlines “AI-generated” lowered belief in them even when the headlines were true and written by people.

challenges.title: Designing AI advice
challenges.scene: People make decisions with help from an AI that is usually right but sometimes wrong. Designers test different ways of presenting its advice.
challenges.question: Which design best cut agreement with wrong AI advice?
options: Showing the AI's confidence with each suggestion
Plain explanations with each suggestion
Making users answer before seeing the AI
challenges.answerTitle: Forcing functions worked, but users disliked them
challenges.explain: Among 199 participants, cognitive forcing designs significantly reduced overreliance compared with simple explainable-AI designs. The most effective designs received the least favorable ratings.
challenges.implication: On high-stakes calls, have reviewers record their own judgment before AI output appears, and plan for user pushback.
challenges.boundary: One online decision task; benefits were larger for people higher in Need for Cognition, who enjoy effortful thinking.

follow.a: Participants higher in Need for Cognition, who enjoy effortful thinking, benefited more from the interventions.
People gave the least favorable ratings to the designs that reduced overreliance most, a tradeoff between performance and user preference.
Three interventions built to compel people to engage more thoughtfully with the AI's suggestions and explanations before relying on them.

challenges.title: Jokes, friends and algorithms
challenges.scene: People rate a set of jokes. Then a stranger, a friend, a family member or a recommender system predicts which new jokes they will find funny.
challenges.question: Which two findings did the study report?
options: The algorithm beat strangers but not friends
The algorithm beat strangers, friends and family
People preferred relying on human recommenders
Spouses and family beat the algorithm
People found the algorithm easier to understand
challenges.answerTitle: More accurate, yet people preferred humans
challenges.explain: Yeomans, Shah, Mullainathan and Kleinberg found recommender systems predicted which jokes people would find funny better than strangers, friends or family did. People still preferred human recommenders, partly because the human process felt easier to understand.
challenges.implication: When launching a recommender, explain in plain terms why it suggests each item; accuracy alone will not win adoption.
challenges.boundary: Joke preferences, a taste domain where humans have many advantages.

study.design: Experiments comparing human and algorithmic recommenders

follow.a: The authors chose a domain where human recommenders have many advantages, which makes the algorithm's win a hard test.
Partly because they believed the human recommendation process was easier to understand than the algorithm's.
Accuracy is not enough. Recommender systems must also be understood if people are to rely on them.

challenges.title: Who saw the STEM ad?
challenges.scene: A firm runs a gender-neutral ad promoting STEM careers and lets the platform's algorithm deliver it cost-effectively. Fewer women than men end up seeing it.
challenges.question: What best explains the gap?
options: Women scrolled past the ads more often
Showing ads to young women costs more
The ad copy appealed more to men
The algorithm learned women click less
challenges.answerTitle: Young women cost more to reach
challenges.explain: Lambrecht and Tucker found that a gender-neutral STEM job ad reached fewer women than men because younger women cost more to reach. An algorithm optimizing cost-effectiveness crowded them out, and the same pattern held on other major platforms.
challenges.implication: Audit who actually sees your recruiting ads and set reach targets by group rather than pure cost optimization.
challenges.boundary: One field test of how STEM career ads were delivered, with the same pattern on other major platforms.

follow.a: No. The ad was intended to be gender neutral; the gap came from an algorithm that simply optimized cost-effectiveness.
The authors report the same regularity extends to other major digital platforms.

follow.q: What does crowding out mean here?
follow.a: Other advertisers value younger women highly, so reaching them costs more, and a cost-minimizing campaign reaches fewer of them.

challenges.title: Do customers notice the AI?
challenges.scene: A firm rolled out a generative-AI assistant that suggests replies to its customer-support agents, in stages across 5,172 agents.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: After agents got AI assistance, customers became less likely to ask for a manager.

challenges.answerTitle: Customers got politer and escalated less
challenges.explain: With AI assistance, customers were more polite and less likely to ask to speak to a manager, alongside a 15% average rise in issues resolved per hour.
challenges.implication: Track escalation rates and customer tone in AI pilots; part of the payoff may show up in supervisors' time.
challenges.boundary: One firm’s customer-support chat operation, with a staggered rollout across agents.

follow.a: Gains were largest for moderately rare problems, where agents had less experience but the system still had enough training data.
The authors find AI assistance facilitated worker learning and improved English fluency, especially among international agents.
The authors report AI assistance improved the experience of work along several dimensions.

challenges.title: How much faster with GPT-4?

challenges.question: How much faster did consultants with AI finish?

estimate.label: Speed gain on inside-frontier tasks

challenges.answerTitle: 25.1% faster, with more tasks done
challenges.explain: Consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks and worked 25.1% faster. Graded quality rose 33.9% with GPT-4 and a prompt-engineering overview, and 29.9% with GPT-4 alone.
challenges.implication: Pilot AI on drafting and ideation first, and measure speed, completion and blind-graded quality together.
challenges.boundary: One firm's consultants on designed tasks for a fictional company; on a task outside the frontier, AI users were less often correct.

follow.a: The bottom-half-skill consultants benefited most, though above-average consultants also benefited meaningfully.
Somewhat. Quality rose 33.9% with a prompt-engineering overview versus 29.9% with GPT-4 alone.
Yes. The same study built a task outside the frontier, where AI users did worse; the "Leading with AI" case covers that result.

challenges.title: Who gets the assistant first?
challenges.scene: A firm rolled out a generative-AI reply assistant to its customer-support agents in waves. You decide which agents get the first licenses.
challenges.question: Which agents gained the most from the assistant?
options: Agents with middling tenure
Newest, least experienced agents
Top-rated, most experienced agents
Agents handling the most common problems
challenges.answerTitle: Start with less experienced agents
challenges.explain: In a staggered rollout to customer-support agents, issues resolved per hour rose 15% on average, and less experienced and lower-skilled agents improved both speed and quality.
challenges.implication: Target early licenses at newer and lower-performing staff, and report gains by tenure tier.
challenges.boundary: Customer-support chat at one firm; gains were largest on moderately rare problems where the system had enough training data.

follow.a: Less experienced and lower-skilled agents improved both speed and quality, which made them the natural first group.
Issues resolved per hour, which rose 15% on average with access to the assistant.
Gains were largest for moderately rare problems, where agents had less experience but the system still had enough training data.

challenges.title: Will your stars get better too?
challenges.scene: In a staggered rollout of an AI assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents, the assistant also reached the most experienced, highest-skilled agents.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: For the most experienced, highest-skilled agents, AI assistance improved both speed and quality.

challenges.answerTitle: Top agents: slightly faster, slightly lower quality
challenges.explain: Across 5,172 customer-support agents, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found that the most experienced, highest-skilled agents gained little from the AI assistant: small improvements in speed, alongside small declines in the quality of their output.
challenges.implication: Let top performers tune or skip suggestions, and monitor their quality scores after rollout.
challenges.boundary: One firm's support chat; the declines for top agents were small, and other occupations may differ.

follow.a: The earlier steps of this case show which agents gained on speed and quality.

follow.q: Does the AI help experts at all?
follow.a: Slightly. They saw small gains in speed, offset by small declines in quality.
The authors argue the assistant spreads the know-how of the most able agents, which experienced agents already have.

challenges.title: Which tasks go to GPT-4?
challenges.scene: Next, your strategy team gets GPT-4. Their work ranges from brainstorming product ideas to a brand recommendation that hinges on details buried in interview notes.
challenges.question: Assign each task.

tasks.text: Propose ten product ideas for an underserved market
tasks.why: Inside the frontier, consultants with GPT-4 finished 12.2% more tasks, with higher graded quality.

tasks.text: Draft press-release copy for the new product
tasks.why: This was one of the inside-frontier tasks, where AI users produced higher-quality work.

tasks.text: Pick the brand to grow from interview notes and spreadsheets
tasks.why: On this outside-frontier task, correctness fell from 84.5% without AI to 70.6% with GPT-4 and 60.0% with GPT-4 plus a prompt overview.

challenges.answerTitle: Use AI inside the frontier, not outside
challenges.explain: Inside the frontier, consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks and finished them faster. On the outside-frontier case, correctness fell from 84.5% without AI to 70.6% with GPT-4 and 60.0% with GPT-4 plus a prompt overview.
challenges.implication: Test each task type for convincing AI errors before rollout; keep humans in charge where those errors appear.
challenges.boundary: One designed outside-frontier task for a fictional company; the frontier moves as models change.

follow.q: Did prompt training help on the hard task?
follow.a: No. The group with a prompt-engineering overview was correct about 60% of the time, below GPT-4 alone at 70.6%.

follow.q: How was the hard task built?
follow.a: Success required a careful review of interview notes that held the key details, then advice to the CEO on which brand held the most growth potential.
758 BCG consultants, randomized to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 with a prompt-engineering overview.

challenges.title: Tutoring with GPT-4
challenges.scene: HR proposes unrestricted ChatGPT-style access in new-hire training. In a related field experiment, high school students practiced math with GPT-4, then took exams without it.
challenges.question: How did unrestricted-AI students score on unaided exams versus controls?

estimate.label: Change in exam grades vs students without AI

challenges.answerTitle: 17% lower on exams without AI
challenges.explain: Practice grades rose 48% with plain GPT-4, but exam grades fell 17% versus students never given access. A tutor version with safeguards showed no measurable exam harm.
challenges.implication: In training, use AI tutors that give hints rather than answers, and test skills without AI before certifying anyone.
challenges.boundary: Nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey over four 90-minute sessions.

follow.q: What were students doing with it?
follow.a: Most used plain GPT-4 to obtain solutions; the most common message was 'What is the answer?'
No. Students in the plain GPT-4 arm did not perceive that they performed worse or learned less.

follow.q: What did the tutor version change?
follow.a: It added safeguards such as hints instead of answers and teacher-provided solutions. Practice grades rose 127%, and exam scores matched controls.

challenges.title: Measuring ad lift
challenges.scene: Your agency compares Facebook users who saw a campaign with users who did not, after matching on demographics and behavior. A randomized holdout ran at the same time.
challenges.question: How did the matched estimates compare with the randomized tests across 15 campaigns?
options: They matched the randomized lift
They understated the lift by a steady margin
They matched once enough data were added
They often missed the randomized lift
challenges.answerTitle: Matching often missed the experiment’s answer
challenges.explain: Across 15 Facebook ad experiments with 1.6 billion impressions, observational methods often failed to reproduce the randomized estimates, even after conditioning on extensive demographic and behavioral data.
challenges.implication: Keep a randomized holdout for major campaigns before trusting matched or platform-reported lift numbers.
challenges.boundary: Fifteen US Facebook campaigns; observational methods both over- and underestimated lift across campaigns.

follow.a: Fifteen US advertising RCTs run at Facebook, covering about 500 million user-experiment observations and 1.6 billion impressions.
No. Across the 15 experiments, observational methods often failed to match the randomized results, even with rich demographic and behavioral data.
Mostly, but not always. In some studies they significantly underestimated the randomized lift.

study.design: 15 field RCTs compared with observational methods

challenges.title: The noisy ROI test
challenges.scene: Your CFO wants a randomized test to prove a digital campaign's return before renewing it. Individual customers' weekly sales swing wildly.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Over 100 percentage points wide
challenges.explain: The median confidence interval on return on investment was over 100 percentage points wide, because individual sales are very noisy relative to ad effects.
challenges.implication: Pool several experiments or measure lower-variance outcomes before asking one test to settle a campaign's ROI.
challenges.boundary: Digital ads for major US retailers and brokerages; the experiments were unbiased, the limit was statistical precision.

follow.a: The experiments represented $2.8 million in digital advertising expenditure.

follow.q: How big would a decisive test be?
follow.a: With a coefficient of variation of sales around 10, which the authors call common, informative experiments can require more than 10 million person-weeks.

follow.q: Does this mean RCTs are useless here?
follow.a: No. Randomization still removes selection bias; the problem is that ad effects are small relative to sales noise, so estimates are imprecise.

study.n: 25 ad campaigns at US retailers and brokerages

forecast.claim: The median experiment’s ROI confidence interval was under 50 percentage points wide.

challenges.title: Save more, later
challenges.scene: Employees save little for retirement and resist raising contributions now. An adviser offers a plan that commits part of each future pay raise to savings.
challenges.question: Participants started at a 3.5% savings rate. Where were they after four raises?

estimate.label: Average savings rate after four pay raises

challenges.answerTitle: Savings rates rose from 3.5% to 13.6%
challenges.explain: In the first implementation, participants' savings rates increased from 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent over 40 months, and 78 percent of those offered the plan joined.
challenges.implication: Offer a sign-up that raises retirement contributions at each future raise, so take-home pay never falls.
challenges.boundary: Early company implementations with employees who chose to join.

follow.a: 78 percent of those offered the plan joined.
Few did. 80 percent of those enrolled remained in it through the fourth pay raise.
Employees commit in advance to allocating part of future salary increases to saving, so the extra saving starts when pay goes up rather than out of current take-home pay.

study.n: Employees offered the plan at the first implementing firm

challenges.title: Thesis deadlines
challenges.scene: Senior honors students gave their most realistic date for finishing their thesis, plus a best-case and a worst-case date. Researchers then tracked when they actually finished.
challenges.question: What share finished by their own most realistic date?

estimate.label: Share finishing by their best-guess date

challenges.answerTitle: Fewer than one in three finished on time
challenges.explain: Only 29.7% finished by their best-guess date, against an average prediction of 33.9 days, and fewer than half (48.7%) finished by their worst-case date.
challenges.implication: Set project deadlines from how long similar past projects actually took, not from the team's step-by-step plan.
challenges.boundary: Study 1 tracked psychology honors students on their theses; one task type, one university.

follow.a: Not reliably. Only 48.7% finished by the date they predicted if everything went as poorly as it possibly could.

follow.q: How far off was the average?
follow.a: Students predicted 33.9 days on average; actual completion took about three weeks longer.
Later studies in the paper point to focusing on plans for the future while discounting past experience with similar tasks.

challenges.title: Shirking from home?
challenges.scene: Ctrip, a 16,000-employee Chinese travel agency, asked call-center staff to volunteer for home working, then randomly assigned volunteers to home or office for nine months.
challenges.question: By how much did home workers' performance change?

estimate.label: Change in performance when working from home

challenges.answerTitle: Performance rose 13%
challenges.explain: Home working led to a 13% performance increase, 9% of it from working more minutes per shift, and attrition roughly halved.
challenges.implication: Pilot remote work on roles with measurable output, assign it randomly, and judge it on output rather than presence.
challenges.boundary: Volunteer call-center staff with easily measured output; home workers' promotion rate, given performance, fell.

follow.q: Where did the gain come from?
follow.a: Nine of the 13 points came from working more minutes per shift; the rest from more calls per minute, which the authors attribute to a quieter, more convenient setting.

follow.q: What happened when it went company-wide?
follow.a: Over half of employees switched their choice, and the gains from working from home almost doubled to 22%, which the authors attribute to learning and selection.
Yes. Conditional on performance, home workers' promotion rate fell.

study.n: Volunteer call-center staff at Ctrip, 9 months

challenges.title: Mugs, sellers and buyers
challenges.scene: In classic classroom markets, students given a mug asked a median $7.12 to sell it, while buyers offered $2.87. Plott and Zeiler reran the design with training, practice rounds and anonymous offers.
challenges.question: What happened to the gap between sellers and buyers?
challenges.answerTitle: Under careful procedures, the mug gap disappeared
challenges.explain: Sellers’ median of $7.12 against buyers’ $2.87 in the original markets gave way to no gap under Plott and Zeiler’s procedures. Isoni, Loomes and Sugden later confirmed this for mugs but found a persistent gap for lotteries.
challenges.implication: Before pricing on an "owners overvalue" story, test it with clear instructions and practice; the effect depends on how the choice is elicited.
challenges.boundary: Student markets for mugs under two elicitation procedures, with the follow-up debate extending to lotteries.

follow.q: Did the gap reduce trading in the 1990 markets?
follow.a: Yes. While 12.5 trades were expected between buyers and sellers, only three took place.
Buyers and choosers gave similar values, so Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler read the gap as reluctance to give up the mug, not reluctance to spend.

follow.q: Is the gap just a quirk of the procedure?
follow.a: Debated. Plott and Zeiler (2005) made the mug gap disappear with procedures that remove misunderstandings; Isoni, Loomes and Sugden (2011) confirmed that for mugs but found a persistent gap for lotteries under the same procedures.

options: It disappeared
It stayed about as large
It shrank by about half
It reversed: buyers valued more

challenges.title: Who stays with hybrid?
challenges.scene: Trip.com randomized 1,612 engineering, marketing and finance staff. Those with odd-numbered birthdays could work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays; the rest stayed in the office full time.
challenges.question: By how much did hybrid work cut the quit rate overall?
challenges.answerTitle: Quits fell by a third, with no loss in performance
challenges.explain: Hybrid work cut quit rates by one-third (7.20% to 4.80%), with larger drops for women and non-managers. Performance reviews showed no difference over two years.
challenges.implication: Offer two home days a week in high-attrition roles, and track performance reviews to confirm nothing is lost.
challenges.boundary: One Chinese technology firm: a six-month randomized trial with 1,612 employees, with performance reviews over two years.

follow.a: No. Reviews across four half-year periods showed no difference between groups, and equivalence tests supported a null effect.
No evidence of a difference in promotions, and for 653 engineers no difference in daily lines of code.

challenges.title: Fines for late pickup
challenges.scene: In a famous field experiment, ten Israeli day-care centers tracked late pickups for 20 weeks. In week 5, six centers began fining parents NIS 10 for arriving 10+ minutes late. In week 17 the fine was dropped.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: After the fine was removed, late pickups stayed at the higher level they had reached while the fine applied.

challenges.answerTitle: Lateness nearly doubled and stayed high
challenges.explain: In Gneezy and Rustichini's six fined day-care centers, late pickups settled at almost twice the pre-fine rate and stayed there after the fine ended (center 1: 7.25 a week before, 15.25 after). The four control centers did not change.
challenges.implication: Before fining a behavior, ask whether the fine turns a social obligation into a price people will happily pay.
challenges.boundary: A small fine in ten day-care centers over 20 weeks; four control centers showed no change.

follow.a: Yes. In the four centers without a fine, no noticeable change took place after the fourth week, or in any other week.
NIS 10 per child for parents arriving 10 or more minutes late.
The authors observed a steady increase after the fine began, until the rate settled almost twice as large as the initial one.

challenges.title: Photo or price?
challenges.scene: A consumer lender mailed loan offers to clients, randomizing the interest rate along with ad content such as a photo, the number of example loans and the offer deadline.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: A photo of an attractive woman raised loan demand far less than a 25% interest-rate cut did.

Demand strongly increased with longer deadlines, contrary to the idea that short deadlines help people who procrastinate.
The authors read the evidence as ads persuading by appealing peripherally to intuition rather than to reason.
