challenges.title: More options on the shelf
challenges.scene: A famous grocery study found about 30% of shoppers who stopped at the display bought jam after a 6-flavor display versus 3% after a 24-flavor display. Your team proposes cutting your product range.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Across 50 experiments, more options reduced choice or satisfaction on average.

challenges.answerTitle: On average, the effect is near zero
challenges.explain: A meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 experiments (5,036 participants) found a mean effect size of virtually zero (D = 0.02), with considerable variance between studies.
challenges.implication: Test a range cut in your own category before assuming fewer options will sell more.
challenges.boundary: Large variance between studies: overload appears in some settings and is absent in others.

follow.q: What did the jam study find exactly?
follow.a: More shoppers stopped at the 24-jam table, but about 30% of those who saw 6 jams bought one, versus 3% of those who saw 24.
63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished experiments, with 5,036 participants.

follow.q: So was the jam study wrong?
follow.a: Not necessarily. The meta-analysis found considerable variance between studies, so single results like the jam study coexist with an average near zero.

challenges.title: Sign here first?
challenges.scene: A 2012 PNAS study reported that signing an honesty statement at the top of a form, rather than the bottom, reduced dishonest reports. Government agencies adopted the practice.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: The replications found no effect of signing first on honest reporting.

challenges.answerTitle: No effect of signing first
challenges.explain: Across five conceptual replications (n = 4,559) and a preregistered direct replication (n = 1,235), the authors observed no effect of signing first on honest reporting. PNAS retracted the 2012 paper in 2021.
challenges.implication: Before rolling out a published nudge, check for replications and retractions, then pilot it on your own forms.
challenges.boundary: Tests one form-design nudge on experimental self-reports.

follow.a: The replication team included all five authors of the 2012 paper, alongside Kristal and Whillans.
PNAS retracted the original paper in 2021.

follow.q: Why did a failed replication matter so much?
follow.a: The authors note that government agencies had adopted the practice, so they argued the scientific record needed updating.

challenges.title: When salaries go public
challenges.scene: A new website published University of California employees' pay. Researchers told a random subset of staff about the site, then surveyed everyone on job satisfaction and job search.
challenges.question: What did learning about peers' pay do?
options: Above-median earners: more satisfied
Above-median earners: happier, job hunting less
Below-median earners: less satisfied, job hunting
Below-median earners: more motivated to catch up
challenges.answerTitle: Below-median earners grew unhappy and started looking
challenges.explain: Card, Mas, Moretti and Saez found that below-median University of California earners told about the salary website became 4.3 percentage points more likely to report being very likely to seek a new job, a 20% rise. Above-median earners were unaffected.
challenges.implication: Before publishing pay data, prepare clear explanations of pay differences for below-median staff, who carry the morale cost.
challenges.boundary: University of California employees; outcomes were self-reported satisfaction and job-search intentions.

dag.alt: A random notice about the website changes who knows peers' pay, which affects satisfaction. Unobserved traits such as ability and fit drive both pay rank and satisfaction, which is why a simple survey correlation between rank and satisfaction is confounded.

follow.q: Why randomize who heard about the site?
follow.a: Low-paid staff differ from high-paid staff in many ways. Randomizing who learned about the site isolates the effect of the information itself.

follow.q: Did higher earners gain from learning they earn more?
follow.a: No. Workers paid above the median were unaffected.

follow.q: Does pay level or pay rank matter more?
follow.a: Rank. Responses tracked a worker's rank in the pay distribution more closely than relative pay level.

challenges.title: Pay by rank
challenges.scene: For a month, Indian manufacturing workers in production teams were randomly paid either the same flat daily wage or different wages based on their baseline productivity rank.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Output fell 0.45 SD; attendance fell 18 points
challenges.explain: When coworkers' productivity was difficult to observe, pay inequality reduced output by 0.45 standard deviations and attendance by 18 percentage points, and weakened cooperation.
challenges.implication: If pay differs within a team, make the productivity basis visible to everyone before the gap takes effect.
challenges.boundary: When workers clearly saw that higher-paid peers were more productive, pay gaps had no discernible effect.

follow.a: No. When workers could clearly perceive that higher-paid peers were more productive, pay disparity had no discernible effect on output, attendance or group cohesion.
Pay inequality also lowered coworkers' ability to cooperate in their own self-interest.

follow.q: How long did the experiment run?
follow.a: About one month, in Indian manufacturing.

forecast.claim: Where coworkers could not easily see who was more productive, paying them unequal wages raised output.

challenges.title: Two ways to compare candidates
challenges.scene: Evaluators chose workers for a task and were paid on the chosen worker's future performance. Some saw candidates one at a time; others compared candidates side by side.
challenges.question: Which procedure made evaluators rely more on individual performance?
options: Seeing candidates one at a time
Comparing candidates side by side
challenges.answerTitle: Side-by-side review focused choices on performance
challenges.explain: In Bohnet, van Geen and Bazerman's incentivized experiment, evaluators who compared candidates side by side relied more on individual performance, while those judging one at a time leaned more on gender stereotypes, so joint evaluation paid evaluators the most.
challenges.implication: Compare shortlisted candidates side by side on the same criteria instead of scoring each one in isolation.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized lab hiring task with clear performance scores; real hiring information is noisier.

follow.a: The authors draw on decision research showing that people reason more carefully when they compare options together than when they judge one in isolation.

follow.q: Does it cost the employer anything?
follow.a: No. Because evaluators picked on performance, joint evaluation was the profit-maximizing procedure.

follow.q: How does it relate to blind auditions?
follow.a: The authors present it as an alternative to blind evaluation, which helped women musicians win orchestra positions but is hard to use in many workplaces.

challenges.title: Organ donor forms
challenges.scene: An online survey asked 161 people whether they would be organ donors. The question was framed as opt-in, opt-out, or a neutral form requiring a choice with no default.
challenges.question: Which form produced the fewest donors?
options: Neutral (must choose, no default)
Opt-out (default: donor)
Opt-in (default: non-donor)
challenges.answerTitle: Opt-out and active choice both beat opt-in
challenges.explain: Consent was about twice as high under opt-out as under opt-in, and opt-out did not differ significantly from the neutral form (79%).
challenges.implication: Where you cannot set a favorable default, require an active choice rather than leaving opt-in as the silent default.
challenges.boundary: Stated intentions from 161 online respondents; the country comparisons in the paper are correlational.

follow.q: Does this show up across countries?
follow.a: Yes. In effective consent rates, nearly 60 percentage points separated opt-out from opt-in European countries, with no overlap.
In a 1999 cross-section cited by the authors, presumed-consent countries had 16.9 donations per million versus 10.8 in explicit-consent countries.

follow.q: Why does the default matter so much?
follow.a: The authors argue that if preferences about donation were strong, defaults should have little effect; the large gap suggests many people hold weak preferences.

challenges.title: Fund menus and real plans
challenges.scene: Benartzi and Thaler (2001) reported that the share invested in stocks rose with the share of stock funds on a 401(k) menu. Huberman and Jiang (2006) then examined administrative records of participants in many real 401(k) plans.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: In real plans, the menu’s mix mattered little
challenges.explain: Huberman and Jiang found that participants split contributions evenly across the funds they use, typically three or four, yet their propensity to put money into equity funds was not very sensitive to the fraction of equity funds offered.
challenges.implication: Before redesigning a plan menu to steer risk, check your own participants’ records; in large real-plan data, equity exposure moved little with the menu’s mix.
challenges.boundary: Administrative records of 401(k) participants across many plans, set against earlier evidence from hypothetical allocation tasks and plan-level comparisons.

follow.q: What did the original study find?
follow.a: Benartzi and Thaler reported that some investors split contributions evenly across whatever funds are offered, so the stock share rose with the share of stock funds on the menu.
The designs differ: hypothetical allocation tasks and comparisons across plans, versus records of individual participants inside real plans.

follow.q: Does the even split still happen?
follow.a: Yes. Participants tend to allocate evenly across the funds they use, but they use only a few, and that number does not track how many are offered.

forecast.claim: In real plans, more equity funds on the menu meant more money in equity.

challenges.title: Lost wallets, different contents
challenges.scene: Researchers handed 'lost' wallets to staff at banks, hotels, post offices and police stations. In the US, UK and Poland, wallets held no money, US$13.45, or US$94.15.
challenges.question: Rank the wallets by how often staff contacted the owner.
options: US$94.15 in cash
No money
US$13.45 in cash
challenges.rankLabel: Share of wallets reported to the owner
challenges.answerTitle: More money, more wallets returned
challenges.explain: Reporting rose from 46% with no money to 61% with US$13.45 and 72% with US$94.15. Across all 40 countries, money raised reporting from 40% to 51%.
challenges.implication: When designing controls, make the owner and the stakes visible; people resist taking more when it would clearly feel like theft.
challenges.boundary: Wallets handed to counter staff in 355 cities; return was measured by owner emails, a measure later questioned for cross-country rankings.

follow.q: Did the key in the wallet matter?
follow.a: Yes. Wallets with a key, useful only to the owner, were more likely to be reported, which the authors read as concern for the owner.

follow.q: Did this hold in every country?
follow.a: The money effect appeared in 38 of 40 countries, and no country showed a significant drop in reporting when money was added.
17,303 wallets were turned in across 355 cities in 40 countries, typically five to eight of each country's largest cities.

chart.note: Share of lost wallets reported, three countries pooled.

challenges.title: What the experts expected
challenges.scene: Researchers asked 279 academic economists and 299 other survey respondents to predict how adding cash to a lost wallet would change US return rates.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Fewer than half of the surveyed economists predicted that return rates would rise with more money.

challenges.answerTitle: Fewer than a third of economists foresaw the pattern
challenges.explain: Among 279 economists, 49% predicted a decrease and 29% an increase; among 299 laypeople, 18% predicted an increase.
challenges.implication: Pilot honesty controls before scaling them; expert intuition about how people respond to temptation got the direction wrong here.
challenges.boundary: Predictions were for US return rates; actual behavior came from the 40-country field experiment with wallets handed to counter staff.

follow.a: They expected reporting to fall as money increased, from 73% with no money to 65% with a modest sum and 55% with a substantial sum.
Their errors were smaller, but they predicted roughly flat rates of 69%, 69% and 66%.

follow.q: Why might the experts have missed it?
follow.a: They expected self-interest to win out. The authors trace the rise to concern for the owner combined with an aversion to seeing oneself as a thief.

chart.note: Share who predicted more money would raise reporting.

challenges.title: How much do people lie?
challenges.scene: Across many experiments, people privately rolled a die or flipped a coin and reported the result. Higher reports paid more, and nobody could check.
challenges.question: What share of the possible gains from lying did people leave on the table?

estimate.label: Share of potential lying gains forgone

challenges.answerTitle: About three-quarters of possible gains forgone
challenges.explain: Pooling 270,616 decisions by 44,390 subjects, the average standardized report was only 0.234: subjects forgo about three-quarters of the potential gains from lying.
challenges.implication: For self-reported claims such as expenses or hours, assume most people report honestly and aim checks at the minority who inflate.
challenges.boundary: Lab and online reporting tasks with modest stakes; raising incentives changed behavior very little within these studies.

follow.q: Why do people pass up free money?
follow.a: The authors' new experiments point to two main motives: a preference for being honest and a preference for being seen as honest.

follow.q: Do bigger stakes produce more lying?
follow.a: Barely. Subjects continued to refrain from lying maximally when stakes increased, and incentives affected behavior only very little.

follow.q: How large is the evidence base?
follow.a: Experimental studies from economics, psychology and sociology, covering 270,616 decisions by 44,390 subjects.

challenges.title: Honest, liar, or in between
challenges.scene: Lab participants rolled a die in private and reported the number for cash. Nobody could verify any individual roll.
challenges.question: What share of participants did researchers estimate were fully honest?

estimate.label: Estimated share of honest participants

challenges.answerTitle: About 39% honest, about 20% full liars
challenges.explain: The authors estimate that 39% of subjects were fully honest and about 20% of inexperienced subjects lied to the fullest extent; others lied without claiming the top payoff.
challenges.implication: Design expense or time reporting so moderate inflation, not only extreme claims, meets a check or a reminder.
challenges.boundary: One-shot lab die task; the shares are inferred from the distribution of reports.

follow.q: How can they know who lied?
follow.a: They cannot see individual rolls. They compare the distribution of reports with what a fair die produces, which bounds the shares of honest and fully dishonest people.
The authors discuss several motives for this pattern; the study itself measures how many people lie, and by how much.

follow.q: Why does partial lying matter for managers?
follow.a: Because some people lie without maximizing income, controls that only flag the most extreme claims miss part of the dishonesty the study documents.

challenges.title: Corruption and the die cup
challenges.scene: Students in 23 countries rolled a die twice in a cup and were paid for reporting the first roll. Their countries differed in corruption, tax evasion and political fraud.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: In high rule-violation societies, the extra dishonesty came mainly from people claiming the maximum payoff.

challenges.answerTitle: More rule-bending, not more maximal cheating
challenges.explain: Mean claims were 3.17 in low-violation pools and 3.53 in high-violation pools, near the 3.47 'justified dishonesty' benchmark; the share claiming the maximum was unrelated to rule violations.
challenges.implication: Where rule-breaking is common, expect small self-justified stretching more than brazen fraud; remove ambiguity people use to rationalize.
challenges.boundary: 2,568 students in 23 countries; a cross-society correlation with a country index measured years earlier.

follow.a: Reporting the higher of the two rolls instead of the first, a self-justifiable lie. Its benchmark average is 3.47, close to the 3.53 claimed in high-violation societies.

follow.q: How many people were fully honest?
follow.a: An estimated 48.9% on average, ranging from 4.3% to 87% across subject pools, with fewer fully honest people in high-violation societies.
A country index combining political fraud, tax evasion and corruption, based on data from 2003; the experiments ran at least eight years later.

chart.note: Average amount claimed in the die-roll task.

challenges.title: One sentence in a tax letter
challenges.scene: The UK tax authority sent reminder letters to over 200,000 people with overdue tax. Letters varied one added message: social norms, public services, or loss versus gain framing.
challenges.question: Which two findings did these field experiments report?
options: Loss framing beat gain framing
Injunctive norms beat descriptive norms in the letters
Norm messages backfired overall
Public-services messages raised payment rates
Social norm messages raised payment rates
challenges.answerTitle: Norm and public-services lines raised payments
challenges.explain: Across more than 200,000 UK taxpayers, adding social norm messages to standard reminders increased payment of overdue tax; public-services messages also helped, and loss framing did no better.
challenges.implication: In compliance reminders, state accurately what most peers do and what the money funds, and test wording on real payment data.
challenges.boundary: UK taxpayers with overdue Self Assessment debts; outcomes were short-run payment, which accelerated revenue rather than proving lasting compliance.

follow.q: Which kind of norm worked better?
follow.a: Descriptive norms, which state what most people do, appeared more effective than injunctive norms about what people ought to do.
No. The authors found no evidence that loss framing is more effective than gain framing.
No. The authors report that the experiments accelerated the collection of tax revenue at little cost.

challenges.title: Follow the other side
challenges.scene: Researchers paid frequent Twitter users who identified as Democrats or Republicans to follow, for one month, a bot retweeting elected officials and opinion leaders from the other party.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Republicans who followed a liberal bot became more conservative afterward.

challenges.answerTitle: Republicans moved right; Democrats barely moved
challenges.explain: For Republicans the intent-to-treat effect was 0.12 points toward conservatism on a seven-point scale, rising to 0.60 among full compliers; the Democrats' shift was small and not significant.
challenges.implication: Do not expect that feeding a divided team the other side's messages builds understanding.
challenges.boundary: Party-identified US adults using Twitter at least three times weekly, paid to follow a bot for one month in late 2017.

follow.a: 1,652 respondents were recruited (901 Democrats, 751 Republicans); 697 Democrats and 542 Republicans were analyzed.
They became slightly more liberal, but the intent-to-treat effect (−0.02 points on the seven-point scale) was not statistically significant.
The authors could not identify the mechanism. They discuss more political exposure, exposure to women and minority voices, and an anti-elite reaction as possibilities.

chart.note: Shift toward conservatism on a seven-point scale.

challenges.title: Four weeks without Facebook
challenges.scene: Before the 2018 US midterm election, researchers randomly paid some Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for four weeks and compared them with users who kept using it.
challenges.question: Which two effects did deactivation produce?
options: Better factual news knowledge
Heavier Facebook use once reactivated
Lower political polarization
Higher subjective well-being
challenges.answerTitle: Less polarized and happier, but less informed
challenges.explain: Deactivation lowered the polarization index by 0.16 standard deviations and raised well-being by 0.09, but news knowledge fell by 0.19.
challenges.implication: Before limiting staff social media, weigh gains in mood and calmer politics against lower awareness of current news.
challenges.boundary: Four weeks of paid deactivation among US Facebook users recruited through ads, in the run-up to a national election.

chart.note: Values reported in Allcott et al. (2020, AER), read in the authors' accepted manuscript; effects in standard deviations, treatment minus control.

follow.q: How much time did it free up?
follow.a: Deactivating Facebook freed up about 60 minutes per day for the average person in the treatment group.

follow.q: Did people go back to Facebook afterward?
follow.a: Less than before: post-experiment Facebook use was 0.61 standard deviations lower in treatment than in control.

follow.q: What did people need to be paid?
follow.a: The median willingness to accept to deactivate for four weeks was $100; the mean was $180.

challenges.title: One question before sharing
challenges.scene: Researchers sent 5,379 Twitter users a private message asking them to rate the accuracy of a single non-political headline, then tracked the news they shared.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: A single prompt to think about accuracy raised the average quality of the news sources that users shared.

challenges.answerTitle: A small but real lift in quality
challenges.explain: In the 24 hours after one private accuracy question, users shared news from higher-quality sites. More than 80% of 192 robustness analyses gave P < 0.05.
challenges.implication: Add a light accuracy prompt before staff forward external content internally, and expect modest rather than dramatic gains.
challenges.boundary: One private message to 5,379 Twitter users who had shared links to misleading sites; quality was measured over the next 24 hours.

follow.q: How was the Twitter test run?
follow.a: In Study 7, 5,379 Twitter users who had recently shared links to misleading, hyperpartisan sites got a private message asking them to rate one non-political headline's accuracy; the researchers then tracked what they shared.

follow.q: Why would people share news they doubt?
follow.a: In the survey studies, headline truth had little effect on sharing intentions despite a large effect on accuracy judgments; the authors argue attention is focused elsewhere.

follow.q: What happened in the survey experiments?
follow.a: Rating one non-political headline for accuracy at the start made people more discerning about which headlines they would share, in studies of 727, 780 and 1,268 Americans.

study.design: Field experiment on Twitter plus survey experiments

challenges.title: Who spreads the falsehood
challenges.scene: Researchers traced about 126,000 fact-checked true and false stories that roughly 3 million Twitter users shared more than 4.5 million times between 2006 and 2017.
challenges.question: What explains why false stories spread faster than true ones?
options: The gap appeared for political stories, not others
People shared false stories more than true ones
Bots pushed false stories harder than true ones
Platform ranking pushed false stories up
challenges.answerTitle: People, not bots, drove the faster spread
challenges.explain: Across about 126,000 stories, falsehood spread farther and faster in all categories; bots accelerated true and false news at the same rate, so humans drove the gap.
challenges.implication: Counter workplace rumors by addressing human sharing, such as fast, specific official updates, rather than relying on filtering automated accounts.
challenges.boundary: Twitter from 2006 to 2017, with stories verified by fact-checkers; it describes how true and false stories diffused.

follow.q: Which topics showed the largest gap?
follow.a: The effects were more pronounced for false political news than for other categories of information.

follow.q: Why might people share falsehoods more?
follow.a: False news was more novel than true news, and the authors suggest people are more likely to share novel information.
Bots accelerated true and false news at the same rate, so they did not explain why falsehood outran the truth.

challenges.title: Private views in Riyadh
challenges.scene: Researchers anonymously asked 500 married Saudi men aged 18 to 35 whether women should be allowed to work outside the home, and to guess how many peers agreed.
challenges.question: What share of the men privately agreed?

estimate.label: Share privately supporting women working outside the home

challenges.answerTitle: 87% agreed, but guessed only 63% of peers did
challenges.explain: 87% of participants agreed that women should be able to work outside the home, yet on average they guessed that only 63% of the other men in their session agreed.
challenges.implication: Before assuming a change lacks support, poll private views anonymously and share the actual numbers with the group.
challenges.boundary: 500 married men aged 18 to 35 in Riyadh, in sessions of about 30; beliefs concerned other men in the same session.

follow.q: What happened when men learned the true figure?
follow.a: In the control group 23.5% chose to sign their wives up for a job-matching service; with the information, 32.0% did.
Yes. Gaps between private views and what people assume their peers think have been documented in many settings, which is why measuring the actual share matters.

follow.q: What does this mean for a manager?
follow.a: Private support can be far higher than people assume; sharing the measured share can free people to make choices they thought their peers opposed.

challenges.title: From belief to job applications
challenges.scene: Half of a group of married Saudi men were randomly shown the true share of their session peers who privately supported women working outside the home. Months later, researchers checked whether their wives had applied for outside jobs.
challenges.question: What happened to wives' job applications three to five months later?
options: Fell, because of social backlash
Fell slightly as husbands pushed back
Rose from about 6% to about 8%, within noise
Rose from about 6% to about 16%
challenges.answerTitle: Applications nearly tripled, 5.8% to 16.2%
challenges.explain: Wives of informed men applied for outside jobs at 16.2% versus 5.8%, and interviewed at 5.8% versus 1.1%.
challenges.implication: Share accurate peer-support data to move stalled behavior, then track actual outcomes for months alongside stated intentions.
challenges.boundary: One city and one cohort of married men; employment itself rose from 7.4% to 9.4%, a difference within statistical noise.

chart.note: Values reported in Bursztyn, González & Yanagizawa-Drott (2020), follow-up survey results.

follow.q: What did men do right after?
follow.a: In the control group 23.5% chose to sign their wives up for a job-matching service; with the information, 32.0% did.
Not significantly: current outside-the-home employment rose from 7.4% to 9.4% (p = 0.235).

follow.q: How wrong were the original beliefs?
follow.a: Men had underestimated how many of their peers privately supported women working outside the home.

study.n: Married Saudi men from the original sessions

challenges.title: They hate us, or do they?
challenges.scene: Democrats and Republicans predicted how the other party would react to their own party's actions. Predictions were too negative, and the most inaccurate saw the other side as obstructionist.
challenges.question: What best shows the inaccuracy itself drives obstructionism beliefs?
options: Randomly correcting beliefs cut obstructionism ratings
The same bias appeared in a national sample
The most inaccurate partisans were also the most hostile
Inaccuracy tracked heavy political news consumption

dag.alt: Partisanship may drive both inaccurate meta-perceptions and obstructionism beliefs; a randomized correction changes meta-perceptions directly and tests the questioned link.

challenges.answerTitle: Correcting beliefs cut obstructionism attributions
challenges.explain: Across 4,282 participants, people overestimated out-group negativity; in an experiment with 1,122 people, showing true out-group reactions significantly reduced perceived obstructionism.
challenges.implication: In a divided team, collect each side's actual reactions to a proposal and share them before anyone assumes deliberate blocking.
challenges.boundary: Found in competitive intergroup contexts; the correction was tested in one online experiment with 1,122 participants.

follow.q: Does this happen in cooperative settings?
follow.a: No. The negativity bias appeared across competitive but not cooperative intergroup contexts.

follow.q: Who benefited most from the correction?
follow.a: The intervention was more effective for people whose meta-perceptions were more inaccurate.

follow.q: How far off were the predictions?
follow.a: In the correction experiment, average inaccuracy was 22 points on a 100-point scale.

challenges.title: Alone, crowd, or team
challenges.scene: In a two-year geopolitical forecasting tournament, volunteers were randomly assigned to forecast independently, in a crowd-belief condition, or in collaborative teams.
challenges.question: Rank the three conditions from most to least accurate.
options: Crowd-belief forecasters
Independent forecasters
Team forecasters
challenges.answerTitle: Teams beat crowd-belief, which beat independents
challenges.explain: In a tournament that began with 2,246 forecasters, teams were clearly more accurate than forecasters who saw the crowd’s beliefs, who in turn clearly beat forecasters working alone.
challenges.implication: For risk forecasts, have analysts work in teams that share reasoning, and score their forecasts for accuracy over time.
challenges.boundary: Geopolitical questions scored with Brier scores, with volunteers in one tournament; the paper reports test statistics.

follow.q: What happened to the best performers?
follow.a: The top 2% from Year 1, 60 forecasters, formed five superforecaster teams of 12 and outperformed all other groups by a wide margin.
Year 1 began with 2,246 participants; of 199 questions posted, eighty-five (Year 1) and 114 (Year 2) closed and were scored.
With Brier scores, where 0 is the best score and 2 is the worst.

challenges.title: Forty-five minutes of training
challenges.scene: Before forecasting geopolitical events, tournament volunteers were randomly given about 45 minutes of probability training, scenario training, or no training.
challenges.question: Which training produced the more accurate forecasts?
options: Probability training
Neither beat no training
Scenario training
challenges.answerTitle: Probability training beat scenario training
challenges.explain: In a tournament that began with 2,246 forecasters, about 45 minutes of probability training beat scenario training, and training was one of three interventions that raised accuracy.
challenges.implication: Give forecasting and planning staff short training in probabilistic reasoning, and check its value with scored forecasts.
challenges.boundary: Geopolitical forecasts by tournament volunteers; the paper reports significance tests for the training effect.

follow.a: Approximately 45 minutes.
No. The authors treat training as one of several interventions that raised accuracy.
Volunteers in a two-year geopolitical forecasting tournament; Year 1 began with 2,246 participants.

challenges.title: After the hard exam
challenges.scene: In a lab study, 82 students took a hard trivia quiz. Before scores came out, each estimated their own score and their rank among the others.
challenges.question: What pattern does the evidence predict on a hard task?
options: Overestimate own score, think they trail peers
Overestimate own score, and think they beat peers
Accurate on both
Underestimate own score, think they beat peers
challenges.answerTitle: Overestimate their score, yet rank themselves low
challenges.explain: In 18 rounds of trivia quizzes with 82 students, people on difficult tasks overestimated their actual performance but believed they were worse than others; easy tasks reversed both.
challenges.implication: After hard tasks, do not read low self-rankings as humility; compare absolute self-estimates with actual scores before staffing decisions.
challenges.boundary: Trivia quizzes with clear difficulty differences among 82 Carnegie Mellon students; overprecision is a separate bias.

follow.q: What are the three kinds of overconfidence?
follow.a: Overestimation of one's actual performance, overplacement relative to others, and excessive precision in one's beliefs.
People underestimate their actual performance but mistakenly believe they are better than others.
Participants reported distributions over their own and others' scores and were paid with an incentive-compatible scheme, about $20.

challenges.title: Will the mask messages work?
challenges.scene: Researchers tested seven messages (moral frames, mortality, scientific evidence, the economy) to raise mask-wearing among 4,931 US Republicans and Democrats. Beforehand, 1,034 forecasters predicted each message's effect.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: At least one of the seven messages increased mask-wearing intentions among Democrats or Republicans.

challenges.answerTitle: No message worked; forecasters still overestimated effects
challenges.explain: Across 4,931 participants, none of the 7 nudges raised mask-wearing intentions or pledges in either party. Forecasters overestimated the effects overall (z = 4.40, p < 0.001), most of all for Democrats.
challenges.implication: Treat expert predictions about which message works as hypotheses. Run a small randomized test before scaling a compliance campaign.
challenges.boundary: One topic (COVID-19 mask-wearing), US Democrats and Republicans, and seven short messages.

follow.a: Yes. Academics and practitioners made more accurate predictions than laypeople, but forecasters as a group still overestimated the effects.

follow.q: Who was in the forecasting pool?
follow.a: 1,034 forecasters: 611 laypeople from a representative US panel and 103 from the authors' networks, plus 199 academics and 121 practitioners.

follow.q: Did forecasters at least rank the messages correctly?
follow.a: Not for Democrats. Predicted and observed effects for Democrats were negatively correlated (r = −0.63, p = 0.0003).

study.design: Forecasting study of a nudge experiment

challenges.title: Four honesty messages
challenges.scene: Participants read one truthful norm message (what others did or approved of, framed positively or negatively), then reported whether a die roll matched a number they privately chose. Matches paid a bonus; lies were undetectable.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: None of the four honesty messages reduced cheating compared with no message.

challenges.answerTitle: None of the four messages changed behavior
challenges.explain: Among 1,200 MTurk participants, misreporting (winning reports above the 16.67% that honest reporting would produce) hovered around 30 percentage points under every message, with null effects and tight confidence intervals.
challenges.implication: Before adding an honesty statement to expense or reporting forms, test whether it actually shifts employees' beliefs about the norm.
challenges.boundary: One-line messages before a die-reporting game with undetectable lies, in a high-powered preregistered study.

follow.a: A follow-up experiment found the messages did not change norm perceptions, so there was no belief shift to move behavior.

follow.q: Did anyone react to the message?
follow.a: Many participants misremembered the message in a way that supported cheating, and this group cheated significantly more.
No. Neither empirical vs normative content nor positive vs negative framing produced an effect; none of the four worked.

challenges.title: "Everyone does it," they say
challenges.scene: In an incentivized experiment, people could misreport a private outcome for money and were asked what most others do. Researchers varied whether people learned of the chance to misreport before or after stating that belief.
challenges.question: What best explains the link between believing most people lie and misreporting?
options: People who planned to lie projected their own choice onto others
A taste for risk drives both the belief and lying
The belief reflects general cynicism, not the task
Temptation distorts the belief to justify lying

dag.alt: Profit from lying feeds both the belief that most people lie and lying itself; the belief-to-lying arrow may be partly reversed.

challenges.answerTitle: Temptation reshapes beliefs to excuse lying
challenges.explain: Bicchieri, Dimant and Sonderegger show belief distortion: among people asked what others do, knowing a chance to lie was coming raised the share believing most people lie from 38.1% to 62.7%, and winning reports from 21.4% to 40.5%.
challenges.implication: Do not treat "everyone games it" survey answers as facts; check them against actual compliance data and publish what peers really do.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized experiment in which lying paid money and beliefs concerned the other participants.

follow.a: The paper studies two: empirical beliefs (what others do) and normative beliefs (what others approve of), and shows when and which are distorted.

follow.q: Which signal is hardest to explain away?
follow.a: Widespread honest behavior. People read it as a strong sign that lying is disapproved of; widespread lying was not read as approval.
Conditional norm-followers: people who follow a norm only when they believe it applies, and who shade those beliefs when lying pays.

chart.note: Share believing that most people lie.

challenges.title: The open dashboard problem
challenges.scene: Penn students played repeated rounds of a charity game: give to, take from, or leave a donation. One group could see peers' past choices; another could not.
challenges.question: By about how much did donations fall when peers' choices were visible?

estimate.label: Drop in donations vs no visibility

challenges.answerTitle: Donations fell about 20% with visibility alone
challenges.explain: With observation alone, participants took 21.9 ECUs more than in the earlier part of the experiment, and donations fell by about 20% against no observation. People copied bad examples but ignored good ones.
challenges.implication: Before publishing peer compliance dashboards, add even a minimal shared-identity cue among peers; without one, bad examples spread faster than good ones.
challenges.boundary: Repeated giving game with Penn students; proximity was a minimal shared-identity cue.

follow.a: Yes. With a minimal social-proximity cue, extra taking fell to 7.5 ECUs, and seeing peers give raised donations by about 0.20 ECU per ECU given.

follow.q: How strongly did people copy bad behavior?
follow.a: Without proximity, each ECU a peer took cut a participant's own donation by about 0.24 ECU. Seeing peers give had no significant effect.

follow.q: Were the groups different at the start?
follow.a: No. Initial takers were 45%, 44% and 42% across conditions, so the gap emerged from watching peers.

follow.q: Does this match Dimant’s 2019 contagion study?
follow.a: Yes. Both find that people copy bad examples more readily than good ones. Here a minimal shared-identity cue made good examples spread too; in the 2019 study, closeness to the observed peer amplified the spread of bad choices.

challenges.title: Which behavior spreads faster?
challenges.scene: In an experiment, people saw what peers had chosen before making their own pro-social or anti-social choices. The design also varied how socially close those peers were.
challenges.question: Which two findings did the study report?
options: Pro-social individuals were the most easily swayed by their peers
Anti-social behavior was more contagious than pro-social
Closeness amplified bad behavior's spread more than good
Closeness made people copy good and bad choices equally
challenges.answerTitle: Bad behavior spreads more, especially among close peers
challenges.explain: Dimant shows, with 185 lab participants, that seeing an anti-social peer prompted people to revise their choice 33.7% of the time, against 19.4% for a pro-social peer. Under high social proximity the gap widened to 88.2% versus 34.8%.
challenges.implication: In tight-knit teams people copy what close peers do, and bad conduct most of all: act on visible misconduct quickly and make good conduct just as visible.
challenges.boundary: Experiment with pro- and anti-social choices and peers who varied in social proximity.

follow.a: Anti-social individuals were the most susceptible to contagion from other anti-social peers.
By how socially close participants were to the peers whose earlier choices they saw.

follow.q: What is the finding meant to inform?
follow.a: Norm-based interventions: the paper argues its results help design policies that encourage pro-social and reduce anti-social behavior.

follow.q: Does the 2022 proximity study say the same?
follow.a: It fits. Here closeness meant answering personal questions more like the observed peer, and close peers' bad choices spread most. In Bicchieri, Dimant, Gächter and Nosenzo (2022), a minimal shared-identity cue made people copy good examples as well as bad ones, which halted the erosion of compliance.

chart.note: Share who changed their choice after seeing a peer.

challenges.title: Small fine, which message?
challenges.scene: In a trust game, researchers added a weak penalty for returning too little, alone or with a message about what most others do or what most think is right. The cost of complying also varied.
challenges.question: Which combination raised reciprocity?
options: Penalty plus "most others comply," with costly compliance
Weak penalty alone
Penalty plus "most think it's right," cheap compliance
Norm message alone
challenges.answerTitle: Penalty plus normative message, only when compliance is cheap
challenges.explain: With 418 Penn participants, Bicchieri, Dimant and Xiao show that weak punishment plus a normative message raised trustees' returns to 42.7%, against 28.7% at baseline, when stakes were low. At high stakes, punishment plus empirical information cut returns to 22.2% versus 36.5%.
challenges.implication: When a sanction is modest and compliance is costly, do not justify it with "everyone complies"; explain why the rule is right.
challenges.boundary: Lab trust game combining a weak penalty with norm messages at two levels of compliance cost.

follow.q: Why did the costly case backfire?
follow.a: Additional experiments attribute it to the punishment being perceived as unjustified, at least by some people.

follow.q: Did the penalty work on its own?
follow.a: No. In isolation, neither weak punishment nor empirical or normative information increased reciprocal behavior.
Six, systematically combining whether weak punishment existed with no norm information, empirical information or normative information.

chart.note: Share of money sent back to the truster, low stakes.

challenges.title: Who gets reported for bribery?
challenges.scene: US adults read about a coworker accepting a bribe and chose how much evidence to submit, which set how likely the coworker was to be punished. The bribe either created inequity or restored equity; half also learned what most previous participants thought of taking bribes.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Norm information raised punishment of unfair bribes
challenges.explain: Norm information raised the chosen probability of punishment from 73.3% to 82.8% when the bribe created inequity (P < 0.005), and from 57.9% to 67.2% when it restored equity (marginal, P = 0.074). Inequity-creating bribes drew more punishment overall (77.8% vs 62.3%, P < 0.001).
challenges.implication: When you build a speak-up channel, tell staff that most colleagues object to taking bribes; in the study this raised willingness to act most for deals that create unfair advantages.
challenges.boundary: Bribery vignette with 225 US adults, alongside a main behavioral study with 1,240 punishers from a representative US sample.

follow.a: Yes. Lies that created inequity drew 52.8% of the maximum punishment vs 43.6% for lies that achieved equity (P < 0.001).

follow.q: Does the size of the lie matter?
follow.a: Yes. The smallest lie drew 44.7% of maximum punishment, and each larger step added about 10 percentage points.

follow.q: When do norm messages work best?
follow.a: Study 3 found norm perceptions are malleable and norm-nudges are most effective when existing norms are ambiguous.

forecast.claim: Telling people that most others object to taking bribes raised the punishment they chose for bribes that created inequity.

chart.note: Average chosen probability that the coworker is punished, Study 2 vignette. Outlined: the equalizing-bribe difference (P = 0.074).

challenges.title: Giving while watched
challenges.scene: To boost charity giving, an experiment let another person observe each decision to give to a charity or take from its account. In some versions the observer simply watched, with no rewards or consequences attached.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Watching alone did little and could backfire
challenges.explain: Bolton, Dimant and Schmidt show, with 1,650 online participants, that being watched alone backfired: the charity account shrank 28.3% under observation against 18.4% unobserved. Asking people first about others' behavior turned this into a 9.3% gain.
challenges.implication: Do not rely on visibility alone in giving or compliance drives; pair it with a clear statement of what is expected.
challenges.boundary: Give-or-take charity games in the lab and online (1,650 decision makers online), where a decision maker chose with or without a passive observer watching.

follow.a: The authors find that inequality aversion drives the backfiring of observability.
Increasing the salience of norms mitigated the unintended consequences and increased pro-social behavior.

follow.q: Do people care about being observed at all?
follow.a: Yes. Individuals were sensitive to the observability of their actions; observation alone just rarely moved behavior in the intended direction.

forecast.claim: Letting another person watch each donation decision raised giving.

chart.note: Change in the charity account.

challenges.title: Whose example do you pick?
challenges.scene: Before a game where lying paid, US online participants chose whose information to see: a peer reporting more lenient behavior or views on lying, or a stricter one. No political labels were shown.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: They tilted toward lenient peers: about 55%
challenges.explain: Without identity cues, people chose lenient (above-median) peers’ information 54.61% of the time, a self-serving tilt in which sources they consulted.
challenges.implication: When employees pick their own benchmarks or peer examples, default them to representative norm data instead.
challenges.boundary: US participants choosing information sources before an undetectable lying game, with and without partisan identity cues.

follow.q: Did political identity change the choice?
follow.a: Yes. With partisan labels, people chose in-group information 62.44% of the time when it was more lenient vs 58.29% when it was stricter.
Yes. Exposure to information suggesting lying is more socially acceptable increased lying. Views on what is right moved only with information about peers' views, not their actions.
Two experiments: 1,945 participants who chose their sources and 2,414 who were assigned information.

study.n: US MTurk participants in two experiments (1,945 and 2,414)

forecast.claim: Without political labels, people chose lenient and strict peers’ information equally often.

challenges.title: Sharing what you don't believe
challenges.scene: In a multi-round sharing task, participants chose whether to share factual news or conspiracy theories, including ones they did not believe.
challenges.question: What drove sharing of conspiracy theories people knew were false?
options: Habit: they shared whatever appeared first
Expected and received social engagement
A hunch that the posts might be true
Novelty: conspiracy posts felt more original
challenges.answerTitle: Expected engagement drove sharing of known falsehoods
challenges.explain: Ren, Dimant and Schweitzer (N = 4,128) show that engagement drives sharing. When conspiracy posts earned more feedback, the share of people sharing them rose from 17% to 33% over four rounds, while the control group did not change significantly (21% to 17%).
challenges.implication: Do not reward internal posts by raw engagement; recognize accuracy and sourcing, especially when reorganization rumors circulate.
challenges.boundary: A pilot and three preregistered experiments with a simulated social-media sharing task.

follow.q: Did people care about accuracy at all?
follow.a: Yes, but in addition to accuracy, people seemed to value social engagement, and traded one off against the other.
People were very sensitive to feedback in the multi-round task: more feedback for conspiracy posts than for factual news raised conspiracy sharing.
A pilot study and three preregistered experiments, reported in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

chart.note: Share who shared conspiracy posts, Study 2.

challenges.title: Cards on top of cash
challenges.scene: A program paid US veterans cash to return unused opioid pills. Researchers randomly added two reminder cards built on timely reminders, planning prompts and loss framing.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Adding the reminder cards to the cash incentive lowered the program’s cost per pill of medication returned.

challenges.answerTitle: Cards raised returns and lowered cost per pill
challenges.explain: Toma, Dimant and colleagues show, with 512 Veterans, that reminder cards raised the share returning unused pills by 6.88 percentage points over a 24.8% control rate, and cut program cost per pill returned from $15.66 to $12.57.
challenges.implication: Before raising an incentive, test cheap, well-timed reminders that help people act on the incentive they already have.
challenges.boundary: US veterans in one cash buyback program for opioid pills; the cards came on top of the cash incentive.

follow.a: They combined timely reminders, implementation prompts that help people plan the return, and loss framing of the cash on offer.

follow.q: Did more people return pills, or just more pills?
follow.a: Both. The cards raised the likelihood of returning unused pills and the number of pills returned.
It was a pre-registered field experiment with US veterans, published in Health Economics.

chart.note: Program cost per pill returned.

challenges.title: Why won't they cooperate?
challenges.scene: Across 15 behavioral experiments with over 8,600 people, participants decided how much to help, harm or cooperate with others who supported or opposed Donald Trump.
challenges.question: What mainly explained weaker cooperation across the political divide?
options: Genuine unwillingness to cooperate with opponents
Too little information about the other side
Stronger love for one's own side
Low expectations of the other side’s cooperation
challenges.answerTitle: Expectations, more than unwillingness, drove the gap
challenges.explain: In Dimant's public goods games, the share of conditional cooperators dropped by a similar amount for a Trump opponent (72.8% to 59.0%) and for a painting-preference outgroup (73.2% to 62.4%). Expectations differed: people predicted opponents would contribute less.
challenges.implication: In politically mixed teams, share evidence that colleagues on the other side do cooperate before launching joint projects.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized experiments on US polarization around Donald Trump, compared with other social identities.

follow.a: Pessimistic beliefs about how cooperative the opposing faction would be, held before any interaction took place.

follow.q: What is the lever for a manager?
follow.a: Correcting what each side expects of the other targets the source of the gap more directly than appeals to goodwill.

follow.q: How large is the evidence base?
follow.a: Five preregistered studies with 15 well-powered experiments and over 8,600 participants, compared with other political and nonpolitical identities.

chart.note: Share who cooperate when they expect the partner to; the drop is about as large for a painting-taste outgroup.

challenges.title: Pick the middle or a side?
challenges.scene: A representative US sample played a two-player contribution game after seeing how others behaved: tightly clustered, widely spread, or split into two extreme camps.
challenges.question: After a split, two-camp norm, how did people contribute?
options: Far more spread out, toward both ends
Clustered at the safe middle option
Much as they did after a tight norm
Close to the average of what they saw
challenges.answerTitle: Contributions split toward the extremes
challenges.explain: With 1,203 US adults, Dimant and colleagues show that a polarized, two-camp norm produced far more dispersed contributions than a tight norm (variance 2.68 against 1.26). In the authors’ words, in polarized environments most individuals prefer extreme actions despite the strategic risk.
challenges.implication: Report the spread of team behavior, not only the average; a split norm pulls people toward one camp or the other.
challenges.boundary: Two-player contribution game with 1,203 US adults, with the distribution of others’ behavior set by design.

follow.q: What do tight, loose and polarized mean?
follow.a: Tight means low variance in others' behavior, loose means high variance, and polarized means u-shaped behavior clustered at two extremes.

follow.q: Whose behavior is hardest to predict?
follow.a: In loose and polarized environments, personal traits and values played a larger role in what people actually did.
Organizations increasingly use descriptive norms to nudge behavior; the authors show the whole distribution of peer behavior shapes reactions, beyond its mean.

study.design: Online experiment, two-player contribution game (6 treatments)

chart.note: Variance of contributions after seeing others' choices.

challenges.title: Paired gambles
challenges.scene: Offered a sure $3,000 or an 80% chance of $4,000, 80% of people took the sure money. A second group faced the mirror image: a sure loss of $3,000 or an 80% chance of losing $4,000.
challenges.question: What share chose the gamble when both options were losses?
challenges.answerTitle: 92% gambled to avoid a sure loss
challenges.explain: With gains, 80% chose the sure $3,000. With the same amounts as losses, 92% chose the gamble. People avoid risk for gains and seek it to escape a sure loss.
challenges.implication: Expect teams behind on a target to take bigger risks. Review risky catch-up plans with the reference point in view.
challenges.boundary: Hypothetical choices by 95 respondents per problem.

estimate.label: Share choosing the gamble with losses

chart.note: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Problem 3 (p. 266) and Problem 3prime (Table I, p. 268).

follow.a: Yes. Kahneman and Tversky called it the reflection effect: preferences between gambles reverse when gains become losses.
No. These were hypothetical choices. The paper argues people generally know how they would behave in such situations.

follow.q: What else did the paper introduce?
follow.a: Prospect theory: outcomes are judged as gains or losses from a reference point, and losses weigh more than gains of the same size.

challenges.title: Can a chatbot talk people out of it?
challenges.scene: 2,190 people who believed a conspiracy theory described it in their own words. GPT-4 Turbo then answered their specific claims with evidence over three rounds of conversation.
challenges.question: By how much did belief in their own conspiracy theory fall?
challenges.answerTitle: About 20%, and it held for two months
challenges.explain: Belief in the chosen conspiracy fell by about 20% after three rounds of tailored, evidence-based dialogue, and the drop persisted two months later.
challenges.implication: To correct persistent false beliefs among customers or staff, answer each person’s specific claim with evidence. A tailored AI dialogue can do this at scale.
challenges.boundary: Online experiments with 2,190 conspiracy believers, in conversations with GPT-4 Turbo.

estimate.label: Drop in belief in their own conspiracy theory

follow.a: No. The reduction in belief persisted at the two-month follow-up.

follow.q: Did it change other beliefs too?
follow.a: Yes. The dialogues also reduced belief in conspiracy theories the participants had not discussed with the AI.
Each participant described their own theory and evidence, and the model responded to those specific claims rather than giving a generic debunking.

challenges.title: Whose recommendation will customers trust?
challenges.scene: Your retail site can show product picks from an AI engine or from a human expert. Eight experiments tested which source consumers prefer.
challenges.question: For each recommendation, which source should customers see?

tasks.text: Pick a laptop on battery life and specs
tasks.why: For practical attributes, people believe AI recommenders are more competent than humans.

tasks.text: Pick a practical product fitted to one buyer's unique tastes
tasks.why: The preference for AI reversed for utilitarian goals when the pick had to match a person's unique preferences (Study 5).

tasks.text: Pick a vacation spot chosen for sensory pleasure
tasks.why: For hedonic picks, people judged AI recommenders less competent than humans (Studies 1 to 4).

challenges.answerTitle: AI for practical picks; humans for taste
challenges.explain: Across Studies 1 to 7b, people saw AI as more competent for utilitarian attributes and less competent for hedonic ones, and the preference for AI reversed when a practical pick had to fit one person’s unique tastes.
challenges.implication: Label AI picks for practical product attributes; present taste-based picks as expert recommendations supported by AI.
challenges.boundary: Consumer experiments on recommendations, measuring how competent people judged AI and human recommenders.

follow.q: Why do people resist AI for taste?
follow.a: They hold a lay belief that AI recommenders are more competent than humans in the utilitarian realm and less competent in the hedonic realm.
It held across product complexity, number of options considered and transaction costs.

follow.q: Can a firm reduce the bias?
follow.a: A consider-the-opposite prompt attenuated the effect, and framing the AI as augmenting a human eliminated it.

challenges.title: Can a model out-argue a professional?
challenges.scene: Researchers showed 8,221 US adults real articles from covert state-aligned propaganda campaigns, GPT-3 articles on the same claims, or no article, and measured agreement.
challenges.question: With no article, 24.4% agreed with the claims. What share agreed after one unedited GPT-3 article?
challenges.answerTitle: Unedited GPT-3 reached 43.5%, near the originals’ 47.4%
challenges.explain: Agreement rose from 24.4% with no article to 47.4% after the original propaganda and 43.5% after an unedited GPT-3 article.
challenges.implication: Assume cheap AI copy can persuade nearly as well as professionals; review AI-written material for accuracy, not only tone.
challenges.boundary: One exposure to a single article on six foreign-policy-style claims in 2021, with GPT-3.

follow.q: Where did the human articles come from?
follow.a: The researchers identified six articles from covert, likely state-aligned propaganda campaigns originating from Iran or Russia.

follow.q: Did every GPT-3 article make the claim?
follow.a: No. Two of 18 GPT-3 articles did not advance the intended claim; dropping them raised agreement to 45.6%.
Yes. After the survey, respondents were informed that the articles came from propaganda sources and may have contained false information.

estimate.label: Share agreeing after an unedited GPT-3 article

challenges.title: Doctor or chatbot?
challenges.scene: Health professionals, blinded to the source, compared physicians' answers to patient questions on Reddit's r/AskDocs with ChatGPT's answers to the same 195 questions.
challenges.question: In what share of evaluations did raters prefer the chatbot's answer?

estimate.label: Evaluations preferring the chatbot

challenges.answerTitle: Raters preferred the chatbot in 78.6%
challenges.explain: Across 585 evaluations, raters preferred the chatbot 78.6% of the time. Good or very good quality: 78.5% of chatbot answers versus 22.1% of physicians'.
challenges.implication: Pilot AI-drafted replies in patient or customer messaging, with staff review before sending.
challenges.boundary: Public forum answers by volunteer physicians, rated for quality and empathy by a team of licensed health care professionals.

follow.q: How large was the empathy gap?
follow.a: 45.1% of chatbot answers were rated empathetic or very empathetic, versus 4.6% of physician answers.
Yes. Physician answers averaged 52 words and chatbot answers 211, and the authors note length may have inflated empathy ratings.
ChatGPT running GPT-3.5, with responses generated on December 22 and 23, 2022.

challenges.title: What is a coding assistant worth?
challenges.scene: Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm randomly gave some developers an AI coding assistant. Researchers pooled the three field experiments.
challenges.question: By how much did completed tasks rise with access to the assistant?

estimate.label: Increase in completed tasks

challenges.answerTitle: Completed tasks rose about 26%
challenges.explain: Pooling 4,867 developers, access to the assistant raised completed tasks by 26.08% (standard error 10.3%).
challenges.implication: Prioritize coding-assistant licenses and onboarding for junior developers, and track completed tasks before and after.
challenges.boundary: Developers at three firms; single experiments were noisy and varied, and the outcome is completed tasks.

follow.a: Less experienced developers had higher adoption rates and greater productivity gains.
No. The authors say each experiment is noisy and results vary across experiments; the 26.08% figure pools all three.
A random subset of developers at each company received access to the AI-based coding assistant.

challenges.title: Noisier markets, more model trust?
challenges.scene: In nine forecasting studies, people chose between the best available algorithm and other methods, including human judgment, across more and less predictable domains.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: People were more willing to use the best algorithm in more predictable domains.

challenges.answerTitle: Uncertainty pushed people away from algorithms
challenges.explain: Across nine studies (N = 4,820), people were less likely to use the best algorithm in more unpredictable domains. They favored methods with a chance of a near-perfect answer.
challenges.implication: In volatile forecasting, such as demand or markets, report the model's track record against human forecasts, not its average error alone.
challenges.boundary: Nine forecasting experiments with 4,820 participants who chose between their own forecasts and an algorithm’s, under low and high uncertainty.

follow.a: Diminishing sensitivity to error: each extra unit of error matters less as errors grow, so a big miss feels little worse than a moderate one.
They choose methods based on the perceived likelihood of a near-perfect answer and prefer methods with higher variance in performance.

follow.q: How large was the evidence base?
follow.a: Nine studies with 4,820 participants in total, all pointing to diminishing sensitivity to forecasting error as the mechanism.

challenges.title: Are the best freelancers safe?
challenges.scene: Researchers tracked freelancers on a large online labor platform before and after ChatGPT, DALL-E 2 and Midjourney were released.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Freelancers with strong past performance were shielded from the losses.

challenges.answerTitle: Top freelancers were not spared
challenges.explain: Hui, Reshef and Zhou found that after ChatGPT, DALL-E 2 and Midjourney launched, freelancers in highly affected occupations lost both jobs and earnings. Strong past performance offered no protection, and suggestive evidence shows top freelancers were hit harder.
challenges.implication: Do not assume your strongest contractors keep their rates; review vendor mix and pricing in writing and image work.
challenges.boundary: Short-term effects on one online platform after 2022 to 2023 model releases.

study.n: Freelancers on a large online platform

follow.a: ChatGPT for writing-related work and the image generators DALL-E 2 and Midjourney; other image-model releases showed similar effects.
No. High-quality service, measured by past performance and employment history, did not protect freelancers from the adverse effects.
Generative AI may change the role of human capital in organizations and reduce overall demand for workers.

challenges.title: Robot or rival: who replaces you?
challenges.scene: Experiments asked people how they felt about workers being replaced by another person versus by robots or software, for others' jobs and for their own.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: When imagining their own job loss, people preferred being replaced by a robot rather than by another person.

challenges.answerTitle: For their own job, people preferred the robot
challenges.explain: Granulo, Fuchs and Puntoni found that people prefer other workers to be replaced by humans rather than robots but reverse that preference for their own job. Losing out to a machine threatens self-worth less, though it threatens one's economic future more.
challenges.implication: When automating roles, address economic security directly; do not assume staff will be less upset than with outsourcing to people.
challenges.boundary: Online experiments in which people imagined jobs, their own or others’, being taken over by robots or by other workers.

follow.q: Why prefer a robot for your own job?
follow.a: Being replaced by machines, robots or software was associated with reduced self-threat compared with being replaced by another person.

follow.q: Is robot replacement less threatening overall?
follow.a: No. It was associated with a greater perceived threat to one's economic future.
As observers, people tended to prefer that workers be replaced by other humans rather than robots.

challenges.title: Will AI images win the click?
challenges.scene: Researchers generated 10,320 marketing images with seven text-to-image models from 2,400 human-made images, then ran a live ad test with over 173,000 impressions.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: In the live ad test, the human-made image beat the AI-generated images on click-through rate.

challenges.answerTitle: No: AI images won by up to 50%
challenges.explain: In the field study, an AI-generated image achieved an up to 50% higher click-through rate than a human-made image, and 254,400 human evaluations showed AI images can surpass human ones.
challenges.implication: A/B test AI-generated creative against your current images before commissioning new shoots; cost and speed favor the trial.
challenges.boundary: The 50% figure is an upper bound from one field test; results vary by model and image.

study.design: Image evaluations plus field ad test

follow.a: Seven text-to-image models, including DALL-E 3, Midjourney v6, Firefly 2, Imagen 2 and Stable Diffusion XL Turbo.
No. Up to 50% higher click-through is the best case across the images tested, not their average.
The authors note AI can produce marketing content faster and orders of magnitude cheaper.

challenges.title: Which tweets fool readers?
challenges.scene: 697 participants judged whether tweets were accurate. Some were real tweets, others written by GPT-3, and each set mixed true and false claims.
challenges.question: Which two statements match what readers did?
options: Readers took longer to judge GPT-3 tweets than human tweets
True tweets by GPT-3 were judged correctly more often
Readers could tell which tweets GPT-3 had written
False tweets by GPT-3 slipped past readers slightly more often
challenges.answerTitle: GPT-3 helped true claims and slightly shielded false ones
challenges.explain: True GPT-3 tweets were recognized more often than true human tweets (0.84 vs 0.72). False GPT-3 tweets were caught slightly less often than false human tweets (0.89 vs 0.92).
challenges.implication: Fact-check AI-drafted public content as strictly as human drafts; fluent AI text makes errors harder to spot.
challenges.boundary: Short tweets on a fixed set of topics, written with GPT-3 in an online survey; the false-tweet gap was small.

follow.q: Could readers tell AI from human tweets?
follow.a: No. Scores for identifying the source hovered around 0.5, close to chance.
Yes. Readers took 29.14 seconds on average for true human tweets versus 21.02 for true GPT-3 tweets and 19.87 for false GPT-3 tweets.

follow.q: How big was the falsehood gap?
follow.a: Small: 0.92 for false human tweets versus 0.89 for false GPT-3 tweets, P = 0.0032; the authors call the effect small.

chart.note: Accuracy at judging whether tweets were true (0 to 1).

challenges.title: Is the AI penalty real?
challenges.scene: In a series of experiments, people evaluated workers, some of them described as getting help from AI.
challenges.question: What explains the lower ratings?
options: AI users’ work was simply weaker
Raters saw AI users as lazier
The penalty came mainly from managers who use AI
Raters could tell which work used AI

dag.alt: Disclosed AI use leads raters to see the worker as lazy, which lowers the rating, even when the work is held constant.

chart.note: Mean laziness ratings of otherwise identical targets. Values reported in Reif, Larrick & Soll 2025, Study 2.

challenges.answerTitle: AI users were judged lazier for the same work
challenges.explain: In Study 2 (n = 1,203), targets helped by AI were rated lazier (2.50) than those helped by non-AI sources (2.16) or with no help mentioned (2.02), and less competent.
challenges.implication: Before reading ratings as performance, train reviewers on AI-use bias and judge output against the same rubric.
challenges.boundary: Four preregistered vignette experiments with 4,439 online participants rating colleagues and candidates who used AI or other help.

follow.a: Yes. In Study 1, people imagining AI use expected to look lazier and less competent and were less willing to disclose the tool to managers.

follow.q: Did all managers penalize AI users?
follow.a: No. Managers who use AI less favored the non-AI candidate; managers who use AI often favored the candidate who uses AI daily.
Yes. When AI was described as useful for a digital task, the penalty in perceived task fit was entirely offset.

challenges.title: Does tailored AI copy sell?
challenges.scene: 297 participants saw either a ChatGPT ad personalized to their personality or a generic ad, for a weekend trip to Rome and for sneakers.
challenges.question: What did personalized ads change?
options: Lowered spending intent for both products
Raised spending intent for both products
Raised spending intent for the trip, not sneakers
Raised spending intent for the sneakers, not the trip
challenges.answerTitle: Trip spending rose $117; the sneaker effect was not significant
challenges.explain: Personalized getaway ads raised willingness to spend by $117 and were rated more effective; sneaker effects trended positive but were not significant.
challenges.implication: Test AI personalization product by product; start with experiential offers before rolling it out across the catalog.
challenges.boundary: Short ChatGPT prompts with minimal profile data, measuring stated willingness to pay.

follow.q: How consistent were effects across studies?
follow.a: Of 33 message versions tested across all studies, 30 were directionally effective and 20 were significantly so (61%).
Big Five personality traits, regulatory focus, political ideology and moral foundations, in consumer, climate and exercise messages.

follow.q: How much data did ChatGPT get?
follow.a: Very little. All studies used very short prompts with minimal information about each person.

challenges.title: The sales bot
challenges.scene: A company randomly assigned over 6,200 customers to structured outbound sales calls from AI chatbots or human agents, varying whether the bot's identity was disclosed.
challenges.question: Which two results did the field experiment find?
options: Disclosure made calls longer
Undisclosed bots sold as well as proficient agents
Disclosure timing made no difference
Disclosing the bot up front cut purchases sharply
Disclosed bots seemed more knowledgeable to customers
challenges.answerTitle: Bots sold well until they announced themselves
challenges.explain: Undisclosed chatbots were as effective as proficient workers; disclosing the bot before the conversation reduced purchase rates by more than 79.7%.
challenges.implication: Disclose the bot at the start of the call, as transparency rules require, and treat the measured drop in purchases as a cost to manage through service quality, not through hiding the bot.
challenges.boundary: Highly structured outbound sales calls at one company.

follow.a: Customers perceived the disclosed bot as less knowledgeable and less empathetic, though its competence had not changed.
A late disclosure timing strategy and customers' prior AI experience mitigated the negative effect.

follow.q: How did bots compare with new hires?
follow.a: Undisclosed chatbots were four times more effective than inexperienced workers.

case.title: Generative AI in your content team

challenges.title: Artists adopt AI images
challenges.scene: Your creative lead wants text-to-image AI for the design team. A study tracked 53,000+ artists on a major art-sharing platform, 5,800 of whom adopted such tools.
challenges.question: Which two changes followed artists' adoption of AI?
options: Average content novelty rose
Favorites per view rose
Prior originality decided who gained
Output volume rose
Visual novelty increased

chart.note: Rate of earning a favorite per view. Values reported in Zhou & Lee 2024, Results.

challenges.answerTitle: More work, more favorites, less visual novelty
challenges.explain: Adopters produced more and their favorites per view rose from 2% to 3%. Average content novelty and visual novelty both declined.
challenges.implication: Use AI to raise volume, but assign a reviewer to flag look-alike output and reward novel concepts.
challenges.boundary: Artists who chose to adopt AI on one platform; favorites measure peer reactions.

follow.a: Peak content novelty rose slightly (marginally significant), and AI-assisted artists who explored more novel ideas earned better peer evaluations, regardless of prior originality.
The authors conclude that ideation and filtering are likely necessary skills in the text-to-image process.
Artists’ productivity rose 25% after adoption, alongside more favorable peer evaluations of their work.

challenges.title: How much should editors touch it?
challenges.scene: Your team will publish persuasive AI-written articles. A survey experiment of 8,221 US adults tested GPT-3 articles with different amounts of human prompt editing and curation.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: About 53%, against 47% for the originals
challenges.explain: Editing the prompt and choosing the best of three outputs reached 52.7% agreement, above the human-written originals and well above unedited GPT-3.
challenges.implication: Budget editor time for prompt design and picking among several drafts rather than line-editing one draft.
challenges.boundary: GPT-3 articles on six claims from propaganda campaigns, read once.

follow.a: Researchers gave GPT-3 the researcher-written thesis statement instead of an excerpt and edited the example articles on unrelated topics.
Nearly. Editing the prompt alone brought it level with the originals; the small remaining difference was not statistically significant.
Picking the best of three drafts added agreement beyond what prompt editing alone achieved.

forecast.claim: With an edited prompt and the best of three drafts, GPT-3 articles drew at least as much agreement as the human-written originals.
