challenges.title: Label the AI-written reply?
challenges.scene: In an experiment, people described a personal situation and got a reply from Bing Chat or from a person. Some replies were labeled as AI-written, others as human.
challenges.question: What does the experiment predict for labeled AI replies?
options: Labeling replies as AI raises trust and feeling heard
Human replies feel more heard; the label matters little
AI replies feel more heard; the label erodes it
AI replies feel colder, with or without a label

chart.note: Feeling heard, 7-point scale; source and label manipulated separately. Values reported in Yin, Jia & Wakslak 2024, Results.

challenges.answerTitle: AI helps people feel heard; the label undercuts it
challenges.explain: AI replies made people feel more heard than human replies (5.74 vs 5.17), but an AI label lowered feeling heard (5.13 vs 5.81 for a human label).
challenges.implication: Keep the label, but expect a dip; measure customers' attitudes toward AI and have staff personalize sensitive replies.
challenges.boundary: One online experiment with Bing Chat and one-off replies.

follow.q: Was the AI better at reading emotions?
follow.a: Yes. Bing Chat was more accurate than human responders at detecting four of six basic emotions, with no difference for anger or surprise.

follow.q: Who did not mind the label?
follow.a: Recipients with very positive attitudes toward the AI showed no negative label effect.

follow.q: What about colleagues who use AI?
follow.a: How colleagues judge people who use AI is a separate decision in the lab (Reif et al. 2025).

challenges.title: How should staff instruct the machine?
challenges.scene: Online participants privately rolled a die ten times and earned more for reporting higher numbers. They delegated the reports to a machine through one of three interfaces. About 95% reported honestly when they reported themselves.
challenges.question: Which interface kept people most honest? Spread 100 points by how likely each is.
options: Machine set on a dial from accuracy to profit
Machine follows if-then rules you write
Machine trained on example data you pick

allocate.label: Points placed
allocate.valueName: share of participants who reported honestly (studies 1 and 2)

challenges.answerTitle: Vaguer machine instructions meant more cheating
challenges.explain: About 95% reported honestly without delegation. Honesty fell to about 75% with explicit rules, 50% with training data and 15% with a high-level profit goal.
challenges.implication: For incentive-sensitive tasks, make AI agent interfaces require explicit rules, and log the goals staff set.
challenges.boundary: Die-roll task paying 1 to 6 cents per report, with online participants in two preregistered studies.

follow.q: Did letting people choose change things?
follow.a: No. In study 2 delegation was optional, about 50% delegated whatever the interface, and the honesty pattern held.

follow.q: Do AI agents carry out cheating requests?
follow.a: More often than people. Human agents complied with about 25% to 40% of full-cheating instructions; GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Llama 3.3 complied with about 60% to 95%.
Partly. The most effective guardrail was a strongly phrased, task-specific prohibition added at the user level, which the authors note is also the least scalable.

challenges.title: Twenty-two flu-shot texts
challenges.scene: Researchers randomly assigned 689,693 Walmart pharmacy patients to one of 22 flu-shot text reminders or to no message. The outcome was a flu shot at Walmart through December 2020.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: Scientists’ predictions missed: r = 0.03
challenges.explain: All 22 texts raised vaccination over the 29.4% control rate, by 2.0 points on average. Scientists’ predictions did not track the results (r = 0.03) and placed the top text 15th of 22.
challenges.implication: Test reminder copy in large randomized batches before scaling; frame the product as already reserved and send a second reminder.
challenges.boundary: Flu shots at Walmart pharmacies in fall 2020, measured in pharmacy records over about three months.

follow.a: Two texts saying a flu shot was waiting for the patient: +2.9 percentage points, a 9.9% lift. Lay raters tracked results better than scientists (r = 0.60) but still placed it 16th.
Somewhat. After a shrinkage correction for the winner's curse, the authors still estimate +2.7 percentage points, a 9.3% lift.

follow.q: How large was the average effect?
follow.a: The texts raised pharmacy vaccination by 2.0 percentage points on average, or 6.8%, over the three-month follow-up.

forecast.claim: Scientists’ average predictions missed which texts raised vaccination most.

chart.note: Correlation of predictions with actual vaccination rates.

challenges.title: Who should break the news?
challenges.scene: Your firm can present offers to customers through an AI agent or a human employee. A series of consumer experiments tested reactions to offers better or worse than customers expected.
challenges.question: For each message, which messenger drew the better customer response?

tasks.text: A discount larger than the customer expected
tasks.why: For offers better than expected, consumers responded more positively to a human agent.

tasks.text: A renewal price higher than the customer expected
tasks.why: For offers worse than expected, consumers showed higher purchase likelihood and satisfaction when dealing with an AI agent.

challenges.answerTitle: AI for worse offers, humans for better ones
challenges.explain: Across consumer experiments, Garvey, Kim and Duhachek found worse-than-expected offers drew higher purchase likelihood and satisfaction from an AI agent, and better-than-expected offers drew more positive responses from a human, because AI seems to have weaker intentions.
challenges.implication: If bots deliver price increases, review that choice for fairness and disclosure; deliver generous offers through people, where they earn more credit.
challenges.boundary: Consumer experiments on purchase likelihood and satisfaction after single offers presented by AI or human agents.

follow.q: Why does the AI get a pass?
follow.a: Consumers see AI agents as having weaker intentions: no selfish motive when the offer favors the firm, no benevolent one when it favors the customer. That dampens reactions both ways.

follow.q: Can a firm get credit through a bot?
follow.a: Yes, partly. Making the AI agent more humanlike strengthened perceived intentions, giving the firm an avenue to receive due credit for a better offer.

follow.q: Do the authors see an ethics problem?
follow.a: Yes. They discuss ethical concerns about using AI to bypass consumer resistance to negative offers.

challenges.title: Do explanations catch a bad model?
challenges.scene: 457 hospital clinicians diagnosed acute respiratory failure from case vignettes, first without AI, then with AI predictions, half also seeing image explanations. Some predictions came from a deliberately biased model.
challenges.question: Rank the conditions by clinician diagnostic accuracy.
options: Standard AI, no explanations
Biased AI, no explanations
Standard AI with explanations
No AI
Biased AI with explanations
challenges.answerTitle: Explanations did not rescue the biased model
challenges.explain: From a 73.0% baseline, standard AI added 2.9 points, or 4.4 with explanations. Biased AI cut accuracy by 11.3 points; explanations recovered a non-significant 2.3, so pairs within each model type are not scored.
challenges.implication: Audit models for systematic errors before deployment; do not count on explanation overlays to help staff catch bad predictions.
challenges.boundary: Vignettes of acute respiratory failure with three candidate diagnoses, in one survey session, with bias built in by the researchers.

follow.a: The researchers built models that made systematic errors linked to patient characteristics, then showed their predictions to clinicians.
Standard AI raised accuracy, systematically biased AI lowered it, and image explanations did not mitigate the harm from the biased model.
Hospitalist physicians, nurse practitioners and physician assistants (median age 34), surveyed between April 2022 and January 2023.

challenges.title: Does the chatbot help the doctor?
challenges.scene: Fifty physicians had 60 minutes for up to six hard clinical vignettes, randomized to GPT-4 plus usual resources or usual resources only. Researchers also had GPT-4 answer the cases alone.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?
challenges.answerTitle: 76% versus 74%: no clear gain for physicians
challenges.explain: Physicians scored a median 76% with GPT-4 and 74% with usual resources only, a difference that was not statistically significant (P = .60).
challenges.implication: Before judging an AI tool by staff results, train staff to use it or build structured prompts into the workflow.
challenges.boundary: Fifty US physicians working six challenging clinical vignettes, graded on a structured reasoning rubric.

follow.a: Not significantly. Median time per case was 519 seconds with GPT-4 and 565 without (difference −82 seconds, P = .20).
No explicit prompt-engineering training was given, matching current integrations. The authors suggest training or predefined prompts in the workflow could help.
Researchers ran one fixed zero-shot prompt three times per case and graded the outputs blind, alongside the physicians' answers. Its median score was 92%.

forecast.claim: Physicians with GPT-4 scored significantly higher than physicians without it.

chart.note: Median diagnostic reasoning score per case; the physicians’ 2-point difference was not significant (P = .60).

challenges.title: A number shown first
challenges.scene: A classic study found that a high or low number shown before a question, such as how many babies are born per day in the US or how tall Mount Everest is, pulled people’s estimates toward it. A large replication project reran it across many labs.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the study found this?

forecast.claim: Across the replication samples, the anchoring effect held up and came out at least as large as in the original study.

challenges.answerTitle: Anchoring replicated, and larger than first reported
challenges.explain: Across 36 samples with 6,344 participants, Klein and colleagues found anchoring effects of d = 1.27 to 2.60 on four estimation questions, against an overall 0.93 in the original study. Ten effects in the project replicated consistently; two priming effects did not.
challenges.implication: Treat anchors as reliable: decide which number a customer or negotiating partner sees first, and test the choice before you scale it.
challenges.boundary: General-knowledge estimation questions answered by participants in 36 samples.

chart.note: Anchoring effect size, Cohen’s d (unweighted replication estimate per question).

follow.a: Flag priming on conservatism and currency priming on system justification did not replicate; imagined contact reducing prejudice showed weak support.

follow.q: How large was each replication effect?
follow.a: From d = 1.27 for distance to New York to d = 2.60 for babies born, against an overall 0.93 in the original study.
36 independent samples totaling 6,344 participants.

themes.title: AI at work
themes.principle: Generative AI raises average output on tasks inside its frontier and lifts weaker performers most. Outside the frontier it makes confident people wrong, and unrestricted use can erode the skill it replaces.

themes.title: Trusting algorithms
themes.principle: People punish an algorithm’s visible errors more than a human’s, yet often weight algorithmic advice heavily when they cannot see it fail. Control, task type and expertise move the balance.

themes.title: Fairness and bias
themes.principle: Bias enters through the target a model predicts, the market that delivers it and the signals evaluators see. Measured outcomes, not intentions, show whether a process is fair.

themes.title: Persuasion and misinformation
themes.principle: Falsehood travels on human attention. AI can personalize arguments at scale, labels change trust in ways designers do not intend, and small prompts to think about accuracy help a little.

themes.title: Choice architecture
themes.principle: Defaults, frames and anchors decide many choices before preferences do, while menu effects are contested in real plans. The design of the decision is a management decision.

themes.title: Pay, incentives and work design
themes.principle: Money changes the meaning of behavior as well as its price. Pay comparisons, fines and flexibility have effects that the incentive alone does not predict.

themes.title: Measuring what works
themes.principle: Observational lift, expert forecasts and famous single studies often overstate effects. Randomized tests, replications and honest uncertainty protect budgets.

themes.title: Honesty and compliance
themes.principle: Most people lie less than they could, many lie a little, and what they believe peers do shapes both. Enforcement works through norms as much as through penalties.

themes.title: Norms and polarization
themes.principle: The average opinion hides the distribution behind it. Misread norms, polarized expectations and visible bad examples drive behavior in teams and societies, and correcting beliefs can move it.

themes.title: Forecasting and teams
themes.principle: Forecasts improve with training, teaming and scoring, and fail through overconfidence and planning optimism. Whether turn-taking or members’ ability drives group performance is still debated.

paths.title: Leading with AI
paths.blurb: Roll out an assistant, decide who gets it first, route tasks across the frontier, and protect the skills your people still need.

paths.title: AI meets your customers
paths.blurb: Disclose the bot or not, label AI content, personalize ads, answer patients. What customers do when AI is on the other side.

paths.title: When to trust the algorithm
paths.blurb: Formulas against experts, models after an error, and the design choices that decide whether people accept algorithmic advice.

paths.title: Measure before you scale
paths.blurb: Ad lift, nudges, remote work and expert forecasts, each put to a randomized test.

paths.title: Norms, honesty, polarization
paths.blurb: Eugen Dimant’s research on how the shape of a norm, the visibility of peers and political identity change what people do.

paths.title: Design the decision
paths.blurb: Defaults, menus, frames and anchors. Small design choices that move retirement savings, consent and estimates.

paths.title: Pay, flexibility and fairness
paths.blurb: Remote work, pay transparency, fines and biased algorithms. What field experiments say about running people well.

paths.title: Truth, persuasion and AI
paths.blurb: AI debaters, AI labels, detection and the spread of falsehood. How beliefs move when machines join the conversation.
